voyage.name: Plaza de la Bellas Artes
voyage.content: Commonly known as Palace of Fine Arts or Cathedral of Arts in Mexico, host of art events and art exhibitions, along with a number of enormous murals including Diego Rivera's El hombre controlador del universo and Jorge González Camarena's Liberación.

voyage.name: Plaza de la Constitución
voyage.content: Commonly known as Zócalo, it is one of the largest squares in the world, surrounded by historic buildings, including the City Hall and the Cathedral.

voyage.name: Catedral Metropolitana de la Ciudad de México
voyage.content: Next to El Zocalo in the city center. The biggest cathedral in the Americas. Containing many altars, its principal altar is made from solid gold.

voyage.name: Angel de la Independencia
voyage.content: A monument in Reforma Avenue that celebrates Mexico's independence in 1810.

voyage.name: Basílica de Guadalupe
voyage.content: Catholicism's holiest place in the Americas, and the destination of pilgrims from all over the world, especially during the yearly celebration on the 12th of December. It is the shrine that guards the poncho of Juan Diego that contains the image of Our Lady of Guadalupe, and is in the northernmost part of the city.

voyage.name: Ciudad Universitaria
voyage.content: The main campus of the Universidad Nacional Autónoma de México, the National Autonomous University of Mexico. Located on Insurgentes Sur Avenue, it is one of the world's largest universities, with more than 270,000 students every semester. In 2007 it was declared a .

voyage.name: Coyoacán
voyage.content: Historic Colonial Arts district which was home to Frida Kahlo, Leon Trotsky, and Diego Rivera, among others.

voyage.name: Plaza Garibaldi-Mariachi
voyage.content: The square is surrounded by cafés and restaurants much favored by tourists, and in these and in the square itself groups of musicians play folk music. Most of these groups are "mariachis" from Jalisco, dressed in Charro costume and playing trumpets, violins, guitars and the guitarrón or bass guitar.

voyage.name: Paseo de la Reforma
voyage.content: A 12 km long grand avenue built for the Emperor Maximilian's wife in the 19th century. Its name commemorates the liberal reforms of Mexican President Benito Juarez.

voyage.name: Cineteca Nacional
voyage.content: It was the first to screen art films, and is known for its forums, retrospectives and homages. It has four screening rooms, a video and a film library, as well as a cafeteria.

voyage.name: Torre Latinoamericana
voyage.content: For stunning views of the city. Its central location, height (183 m or 597 ft; 45 stories), and history make it one of Mexico City's most important landmarks.

voyage.name: National Museum of Anthropology
voyage.content: One of the best museums worldwide over, it was built in late 1960s and designed by Pedro Ramírez Vázquez. Notice the huge, impressive fountain in the courtyard. It gathers the best collection of sculptures, jewels and handcrafts from ancient Mexican cultures, and could take many hours to see everything. They also have interesting international special exhibits.

voyage.name: Plaza de las Tres Culturas
voyage.content: Examples of modern, colonial, and pre-Columbian architecture, all around one square.

voyage.name: Museum of Modern Art
voyage.content: Here you will find paintings from Frida Kahlo, Leonora Carrington and Remedios Varo, as well as a sculpture garden.

voyage.name: Dolores Olmedo Museum
voyage.content: An art philanthropist left her former home, the grand Hacienda La Noria, as a museum featuring the works of her friend Diego Rivera. At least 137 of his works are displayed here, as are 25 paintings of Frida Kahlo. The premises also feature beautiful gardens full of peacocks and a weird species of Aztec dog. However, the museum is under renovation and is sched to reopen sometime in 2026.

voyage.name: Fine Arts Palace Museum
voyage.content: A concert hall and an arts center, it houses some of Mexico's finest murals and the Art Deco interior is worth seeing alone.

voyage.name: Museo Soumaya
voyage.content: A private museum and collection of many well-known European artists, including an extensive selection of works by Auguste Rodin.

voyage.name: Rufino Tamayo Museum
voyage.content: Contains the works of Mexican painter, Rufino Tamayo.

voyage.name: José Luis Cuevas Museum
voyage.content: Opened in 1992 and is filled with about 1,000 paintings, drawings, and sculptures from notorious artist, Jose Cuevas.

voyage.name: National History Museum in Chapultepec's Castle
voyage.content: The Museum's nineteen rooms contain, in addition to a collection of pre-Columbian material and reproductions of old manuscripts, a vast range of exhibits illustrating the history of Mexico since the Spanish conquest.

voyage.name: Papalote Children's Museum
voyage.content: If you've got kids, they'll love it! Bright, colorful, and filled with educational experiences for children of all ages.

voyage.name: Universum
voyage.content: A science museum maintained by UNAM, the largest university in Latin America. Take some time to wander around the Campus.

voyage.name: Casa Mural Diego Rivera
voyage.content: Contains murals of acclaimed artist, Diego Rivera.

voyage.name: National Palace (Zocalo)
voyage.content: You can see some impressive Diego Rivera frescoes.

voyage.name: San Idelfonso Museum
voyage.content: There are some of Orozco's best frescoes. The temporary exhibitions are usually very good.

voyage.name: Franz Meyer Museum
voyage.content: Display the collections of Franz Mayer, it holds Mexico's largest decorative art collection and also hosts temporary exhibits in the fields of design and photography.

voyage.name: Mexico City's Museum
voyage.content: Great place to learn about Mexico City's eclectic history.

voyage.name: Templo Mayor Museum (Zocalo)
voyage.content: Contains the ruins and last remnants of the Aztec empire. attached to the huge archeological site where the foundations of the temple were accidentally found in the 1970s.

voyage.name: San Carlos Museum
voyage.content: The San Carlos Museum holds some of Mexico's best paintings and exhibit 15th and 16th century paintings.

voyage.name: National Art Museum
voyage.content: The National Art Museum, houses a rich collection of Mexican art ranging from the 16th to the first half of the 20th centuries.

voyage.name: Frida Kahlo Museum
voyage.content: The former house of the painter since she was born to her death, and full of some of her works, and many of her personal artifacts.

voyage.name: Anahuacalli Museum
voyage.content: An impressive modern representation of Mayan architecture, it houses Diego Rivera’s collection of Aztec and other precolumbian cultures' sculptures.

voyage.name: Leon Trotsky Museum
voyage.content: This was the house where Trotsky lived in exile during the last 1.5 years of his life, and was murdered by one of Stalin's agents. Guided tours are provided by members of the Workers/ Revolutionary Party.

voyage.name: Wise Men's day
voyage.content: Most Mexican kids receive toys from the Three Wise Men (Reyes Magos). This is a celebration that pays homage to the aforementioned Bible story. To celebrate it the family gather to eat the "Rosca de Reyes", a sort of bundt cake filled with plastic baby Jesus figures. Traditionally, people who get a figure in their slice of cake are expected to host a feast with tamales on Candelaria Day, February 2. The surroundings

voyage.name: Art Week
voyage.content: Each year in February, the world of contemporary art focuses on Mexico City's Art Week when parties, celebrations, special gallery exhibitions and myriad galas take place throughout the city. The event takes place at the same time as two other major art events, ZsONA MACO, and Feria Material as well as numerous other events at galleries and museums throughout the city.

voyage.name: Independence Day "Yell"
voyage.content: In the evening, the President of the country (or the city mayor) salutes the crowds from the presidential balcony in the National Palace in the Constitution Square (Zocalo) and shouts the famous "Viva Mexico". The Zocalo (and the rest of the city) is decorated with ornaments and lights. This is an incredible expression of Mexican patriotism combined with a party mood. Expect big crowds with a big revelery. If you wan

voyage.name: Independence Parade
voyage.content: In the morning, there is a military parade that runs across Paseo de la Reforma, turns right at Juarez Avenue which later becomes Madero Street and ends at the Zocalo. 15,000 to 30,000 soldiers of the Mexican Army, Navy and Air Force march through the streets displaying its equipment and weapons.

voyage.name: Alebrijes Parade
voyage.content: Alebrijes are brightly colored fanciful animal figures that are one of Mexico's most iconic pop art genres. Each year, enormous Alebrijes floats are created and a parade is held along Paseo de la Reforma and then on to the Zocalo. Pink polka-dotted pigs, Purple-winged dragons, orange dogs with spiked haircuts....these and more will march in the parade. After the parade, the giant Alebrijes will be placed in plazas an

voyage.name: Day of the Dead
voyage.content: Mexico is one of the few countries in the world that celebrates this day (Dia de los Muertos), in which people go to the cemeteries to offer tribute to their departed ones, and decorate their graves with marigolds and bright colors. But this is not a sad celebration, on the contrary, people give family and friends candy treats in the shape of skulls and bones made of sugar and chocolate, as well as delicious bread ca

voyage.name: Six Flags Mexico
voyage.content: Largest amusement park in Latin America. The park is fitted with several million-dollar attractions, including Batman the Ride and not for the faint-hearted Medusa Roller Coaster.

voyage.name: Parque Aztlan
voyage.content: Small urban amusement park in the heart of Chapultepec Park. Park entry is free but rides are paid for individually. Includes a giant Ferris wheel with 40 cabins, a large steel roller coaster, a carousel, and swings.

voyage.name: Estadio Azteca
voyage.content: The largest stadium in Latin America is also the eighth biggest soccer stadium in the world. It's the home of El Tri, the Mexico men's national team, and also home to two of the country's most famous soccer top-tier professional clubs: Club América and Cruz Azul. It also serves as venue for concerts and for occasional NFL regular-season games outside the United States. The stadium is undergoing renovations as it prep

voyage.name: Estadio Olimpico de Ciudad Universitaria
voyage.content: Simply known as "Estadio de C.U." Located south of the city, this was the site of the 1968 Olympic opening ceremony. It is home to Club Universidad Nacional, more often known as Pumas, a soccer team operated by the National University (UNAM). The Pumas began as an amateur team of UNAM students, but are now a top-tier professional team in the Liga MX (though still owned and operated by the university). The stadium hos

voyage.name: Estadio Alfredo Harp Helu
voyage.content: Modernistic baseball stadium built in 2019 for 20,000 cheering fans. It is home field for the Diablos de Mexico, a Mexican League professional team.

voyage.name: Autodromo Hermanos Rodriguez
voyage.content: Built in 1962, this 4.4 km track hosts Grand Prix Formula One and other motor racing such as NASCAR and A1-Grand Prix. The next Formula 1 races are 29 October to 1 November 2026.

voyage.name: Arena Ciudad de Mexico
voyage.content: With a full capacity of 22,300, Arena CDMX hosts indoor sporting events and a wide range of popular music events. It is the home for annual NBA basketball games played in Mexico, and also hosts home games of Capitanes de la Ciudad de México, the country's representative in the NBA G League.

voyage.name: Hipodromo de las Americas
voyage.content: Mexico City's home for horse racing, both thoroughbreds and quarter-horses. There are races nearly every day, with different zones for different budgets.

voyage.name: Arena México
voyage.content: The most famous venue for lucha libre.

voyage.name: Arena Coliseo
voyage.content: Another famous venue for lucha libre and boxing.

voyage.name: Bellas Artes
voyage.content: Opera, traditional Mexican and classical music.

voyage.name: Circo Volador
voyage.content: Alternative music and metal.

voyage.name: Ollin Yoliztli
voyage.content: Home to the Mexico City Symphonic Orchestra.

voyage.name: Sala Nezahualcóyotl
voyage.content: Home to the UNAM Symphonic Orchestra

voyage.name: Polanco
voyage.content: Upscale shopping and dining district centered around Presidente Masaryk and Campos Eliseos streets. It also has several shopping malls.

voyage.name: Altavista
voyage.content: Upscale shopping street.

voyage.name: Condesa
voyage.content: Trendy district full with alternative stores and boutiques.

voyage.name: Centro Historico
voyage.content: The city's oldest shopping district, you can find almost anything here. The old department stores are clustered around 20 de Noviembre St.

voyage.name: Premium Outlets at Punta Norte
voyage.content: Northwest of Mexico City (State of Mexico) in the intersection of Periferico (Mexico Hwy #57) and the Chamapa La Venta highway, near Ciudad Satelite. You will need a taxi or a car to get there.

voyage.name: Las Plazas Outlet Lerma
voyage.content: Mexico- Toluca highway Km. 50 in the intersection with Calzada Cholula in the City of Lerma, near Toluca. You will need a car to get there.

voyage.name: Ciudadela Market
voyage.content: A crafts market where cultural groups from around Mexico distribute their crafts to other parts of the country and the world.

voyage.name: Bazar del Sábado
voyage.content: In San Angel. Every Saturday, artists show and sell their paintings in a beautiful, cobblestoned zone of the city. There are also stores where they sell handcrafts.

voyage.name: Mercado de Artesanias
voyage.content: In Coyoacan on Saturdays, featuring handicrafts from all over the country, and classes for kids.

voyage.name: Plaza del Angel
voyage.content: In Zona Rosa, Calle Londres (metro station Insurgentes). Mostly expensive antique shops, the famous Sunday collectibles market has nearly vanished.

voyage.name: Mercado de Alvaro Obregon
voyage.content: In Colonia Roma

voyage.name: Monumento a la Madre
voyage.content: In Zona Rosa. Sunday art market.

voyage.name: Tianguis Cultural del Chopo
voyage.content: The main flea market for the counterculture in Mexico City. Along Aldama Street between Sol and Luna. Metro Station Buenavista.

voyage.name: Mercado de Antiguedades de Cuauhtemoc
voyage.content: Near Centro Historico (metro station Cuauhtemoc), every Saturday 9AM-5PM.

voyage.name: La Lagunilla and Tepito
voyage.content: Near Centro Historico (metro stations Lagunilla and Garibaldi). La Lagunilla has some of the best antiques, and is a maze of interesting thing, although it is a high crime area with 317 reported robberies in 2006. Tepito is more for pirated CDs, stolen things, and knock-offs. This area is huge and it's very easy to get lost. Shopkeepers are mostly friendly and will point you toward the nearest Metro station. For safe

voyage.name: Chedraui
voyage.content: Mexican owned supermarket, offers you a wide variety of groceries, beers and spirits, beauty and personal care items. They offer in store pickup or delivery. Some stores offer kosher section.

voyage.name: Soriana
voyage.content: If you're staying in the Centro Histórico, a useful central one is inside the Forum Buenavista shopping mall, reachable by Metro Station Buenavista. From Roma and Condesa, you can easily reach the one inside the Paruqe Delta shopping mall (Metro Centro Médico).

voyage.name: Walmart
voyage.content: Also owned by them are the high-end Superama and discount-store Bodega Aurrerá supermarkets. Several throughout the city, including one near the airport. Stock just about everything, much like the supercenters found in the US. An easily accessible one is right next to the Nativitas Metro station (Line 2) on the west side of the Calzada de Tlalpan. Exit the Metro on the west side (toward Calle Lago Pte.) and make a le

voyage.name: Super Kise
voyage.content: South of the city, they sell Korean, Chinese and Japanese groceries.

voyage.name: Mikasa
voyage.content: Lots of Japanese food ingredients, candy and drinks

voyage.name: Kokeshi
voyage.content: Mostly Japanese food stuff but they also sell other Asian foods. They also sell Japanese dinnerware.

voyage.name: Plaza de la Constitución
voyage.content: This square measures 240m long on either side. A huge Mexican flag occupies the center, which is ceremoniously lowered and re-raised each day at 18:00. You may see art exhibits, concerts, demonstrations or all manner of social gatherings taking place here. On New Year's Day, practitioners of Mexico's indigenous religions gather to bless believers for the coming year; Mexican independence is celebrated in the plaza on

voyage.name: Templo Mayor
voyage.price: M$59, free for children under 12 and students with valid ID
voyage.content: The site of the main Aztec temple of Tenochtitlan, it was destroyed by Spanish conquistadors in 1521, who then promptly erected the Cathedral roughly over it – but not quite. Centuries later, nearly completely forgotten, its actual location was discovered by accident in 1978 when electrical workers found a piece of a large stone disc depicting the goddess Coyolxauhqui. This set off a few furious years of archaeologic

voyage.name: Museo del Templo Mayor
voyage.content: This excellent four-story museum was designed by Mexican architect Pedro Ramírez Vázquez, and built in 1987 to showcase the many artifacts found on the site. Highlights include the Coyolxauhqui disc as well as the many thousands of offerings found during the still-ongoing excavation.

voyage.name: Palacio Nacional
voyage.price: Free admission with photo ID (national driver's license is acceptable)
voyage.content: The palace in its current form began construction in 1693 and served as the Palace of the Viceroy of New Spain until the Mexican War of Independence, when it became the executive seat of the President (though today it is no longer his official residence). The walls inside the palace display murals by Diego Rivera depicting the history of Mexico from the pre-Columbian age to the Mexican Revolution. You can also visit

voyage.name: Plaza de la Fundación
voyage.content: This place is allegedly where the Aztecs found the eagle eating a snake on top of a cactus (nopal), the divine sign of the gods to settle down and establish the city of Tenochtitlán. It features a sculpture by Juan Olaguibel made in 1970.

voyage.name: Nacional Monte de Piedad
voyage.address: Monte de Piedad and Cinco de Mayo
voyage.content: This building, which was completed in 1758, was built on the grounds of the house of Aztec emperor Moctezuma and later the residence of the Spanish conqueror Hernán Cortés. The building was acquired in 1838 by the Nacional Monte de Piedad, a pawn shop established in 1775 that still operates today.

voyage.name: Casa de la Primera Imprenta de América
voyage.alt: House of the First Print Shop in the Americas
voyage.content: This building, which dates from 1524, housed the first printing press in the New World, which operated from 1539 until 1560. After this time the building was used for a number of purposes until it was restored by the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana (UAM) in 1989; it now houses a museum displaying some of the first books printed in Mexico.

voyage.name: Plaza Manuel Gamio
voyage.content: Features an open-air diorama of the old Tenochtitlán.

voyage.name: Suprema Corte de Justicia de la Nación
voyage.alt: Supreme Court of Justice of the Nation
voyage.content: This building was completed in 1945 and was designed by architect Antonio Muñoz Garcia.

voyage.name: Catedral Metropolitana de México
voyage.content: The largest cathedral in the American continent. Designed by Claudio de Arcinieaga, construction started in 1537 and lasted for 250 years. Be sure to check out the side chapels where parishioners leave offerings for the various saints. For a bird's-eye view of the plaza, you can take a 40-minute tour (Spanish language only) of the upper levels and bell towers of the cathedral (M$12).

voyage.name: Sagrario Metropolitano
voyage.content: A side chapel next to the Cathedral completed in 1769. The façade is an excellent example of Mexican Churrigueresque architecture.

voyage.name: Templo de San Francisco
voyage.content: This church was started in the 16th century and completed in the 19th century; it was built in the grounds of the zoo of Aztec Emperor Moctezuma.

voyage.name: Templo Expiatorio Nacional de San Felipe de Jesús
voyage.content: Built in 1897 on the site of the former Vasque Church of Aranzazu.

voyage.name: Santa Teresa La Antigua
voyage.content: Built in 1678 and refurbished in 1845.

voyage.name: Templo de la Enseñanza
voyage.content: Tucked away on a side street, this very narrow gem of a church was built in the 1770s and is notable for being an outstanding example of Mexican Churrigueresque architecture. Even more remarkable than the façade, however, are the nine gilt retablos inside.

voyage.name: Templo y Convento de Regina Coeli
voyage.alt: Parroquia de la Natividad de María Santísima
voyage.content: Huge historic church known for its opulent baroque interior. Part of a large Conceptionist convent founded in 1573. The statues and artwork is spectacular as is the gilded altar.

voyage.name: Templo de San Felipe Neri
voyage.hours: public access Mon-Fri 10:30 - 14:00, Sat-Sun mass only, no public tours
voyage.content: Baroque-style church established by the Jesuit order in the late 16th century and completed in 1610. The church is famous for its extensive art collection, some of which is on display for public viewing in an attached art gallery. The art was commissioned by the Jesuits during their first two centuries in Mexico. The collection remained intact when the Jesuits were expelled from all lands of the Spanish Empire during

voyage.name: Alameda Central
voyage.content: Established in 1592, this green garden with fountains and statues is the oldest public park in the Americas. The name comes from álamo, the Spanish word for poplar tree, that were planted here. Much of the current layout of the park, with its starburst pattern of paths around fountains and the central kiosk dates from the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

voyage.name: Plaza de Santo Domingo
voyage.content: The second largest square in Centro Histórico after the Zócalo. It is surrounded by various important buildings such as the Palacio de la Inquisición, Santo Domingo convent and the old Customs House.

voyage.name: Museo de la Medicina Mexicana
voyage.alt: Antiguo Palacio de la Inquisición / Palace of the Inquisition
voyage.content: This museum managed by the Medicine Faculty of the National University shows the history of health care in Mexico. Features a great replica of an old pharmacy and reconstructed labs of influential medical researchers. Signage is in Spanish only. It is housed in the Inquisition Palace, built between 1732 and 1737, which was the head office of the Holy Inquisition, the religious authority famous for torturing heretic p

voyage.name: Plaza Manuel Tolsá
voyage.content: In this beautiful square you can find the statue of Spanish king Charles IV also known as El Caballito (the little horse).

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Arte
voyage.price: Adult M$95; children under 13, people with disabilities, students with a valid ID: free; photography permit (no flash or tripod) M$5, video permit (no tripod or lighting) M$30
voyage.content: Housed in the former Palace of Telecommunications, this beautiful Porfirian-style building was built in 1904 by architect Silvio Contri. The museum presents a permanent collection of paintings and sculptures from the 16th century through the early 20th century, including a large number of very early Mexican paintings. The museum is famous for its enormous and ostentatiously decorated Reception Hall and for its Patio

voyage.name: Palacio de Minería
voyage.hours: Guided tours on Sat Sun 11:00 and13:00
voyage.content: Formerly the Mining College, this building dated from 1792 features an old library and a chapel. It serves as venue for the yearly Mexico City Book Fair.

voyage.name: Plaza de las Tres Culturas
voyage.content: So called because in one city square you can see three different time periods of Mexico City's development mixed together: the pre-hispanic Aztec temple grounds of Tlatelolco, the 16th-century Spanish Church of Santiago, and a modern 20th-century skyscraper, now home of the University Cultural Center Tlatelolco (CCUT) for UNAM.

voyage.name: Zona Arquelógica Tlatelolco
voyage.content: The temple, like Tenochtitlan's Templo Mayor, was built in several layers and is now the site of continuing archaeological exploration; it occupies the largest amount of area, on the north and west side of the plaza. If you're not around for the tour, you can guide yourself along the path (complete with English plaques) that takes you through the ruins, which deposits you in front of the Church of Santiago, on the ea

voyage.name: Templo de Santiago
voyage.content: The colonial church, built by Spaniards immediately after destroying the temple in their conquest of Aztec lands, was constructed using stones "borrowed" from the temple itself. Despite its weathered appearance, the interior is well-maintained and should still hold regular Mass, although doors may not always be open to the public.

voyage.name: Centro Cultural Universitario Tlatelolco
voyage.content: To the south, you'll see the modern-day tower and its adjacent buildings, which were built for the Secretary of External Relations (SRE), now headquartered across the street (though they still have offices in the church's adjoining cloister). UNAM runs the building as a conference hall and cultural center, and has a few exhibits open to the public: Memorial 68 (see Museums, below) and the Blaisten Collection, showcas

voyage.name: Plaza Garibaldi
voyage.content: In this square, groups of musicians play folk music. Most of these groups are "mariachis" from Jalisco, dressed in Charro costume and playing trumpets, violins, guitars and the guitarrón or bass guitar. The square is surrounded by cafés and restaurants that cater to mariachi band enthusiasts.

voyage.name: Museo de Arte Popular
voyage.content: The Museo de Arte Popular in Mexico City is a vibrant showcase of folk art from every Mexican state, housed in a stunning 1920s art deco former fire station designed by Vicente Mendiola. Spread across three levels and five thematic halls, it displays crafts like Chiapas carnaval masks, Oaxaca alebrijes, regional costumes, and Day of the Dead artifacts. An illustrated wall map highlights Mexico’s regional traditions.

voyage.name: Museo Franz Mayer
voyage.content: Housed in an 18th-century building, houses the largest and finest collection of decorative arts in Mexico. The collection, including objects from Mexico, Europe and Asia ranging from the 16th to the 19th century was a donation of German-Mexican philanthropist Franz Mayer.

voyage.name: Museo José Luis Cuevas
voyage.alt: Museo JLC / José Luis Cuevas Museum
voyage.content: Housed in the former convent of Santa Ines built in 1600. The museum's collection features works by Mexican artist Jose Luis Cuevas as well as other modern artists, it also presents works (especially sculptures) from European artists such as Picasso and Rembrandt. The museum's courtyard features an enormous statue called, appropriately enough, La Gigantesca.

voyage.name: Academía de San Carlos
voyage.alt: Museo Nacional de San Carlos / Academy of San Carlos
voyage.content: Housed in a building dated 1785 that was conceived as the Royal Academy of Beaux Arts. It is administered by the National University and features permanent and temporary painting collections. This is the oldest arts academy in the Americas and has trained large number of Mexico's most famous artists. Today, the academy is part of the Universidad Nacional Autonoma de Mexico (UNAM) and only graduate courses are taught

voyage.name: Museo Mural Diego Rivera
voyage.content: This museum was built to house Diego Rivera's famous mural Sueño de una tarde dominical en la Alameda Central ('Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Central'), which the painter created for the Hotel del Prado in 1947-1948. The hotel was destroyed in the earthquake of 1985, but the mural survived and was moved to this location. The museum also hosts permanent and temporary exhibits.

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de la Estampa
voyage.price: M$45 (adults), free (students/teachers/INAPAM members); free admission on Sundays
voyage.content: Features a collection of old engravings and other graphic arts.

voyage.name: Museo Kaluz
voyage.content: Eclectic art museum that straddles the line between traditional artistic styles and the worlds of modern and contemporary art. The museum focuses on works that reflect the history and changing cultural values of Mexico City, a unique collection in a city crowded with outstanding arts venues. The museum itself is housed in a historic building, originally the Hospedería de Santo Tomás de Villanueva, but known to genera

voyage.name: Museo de la Arte de SHCP
voyage.content: Eclectic art collection owned by the government's Finance ministry. Mexico has an innovative tax program that allows collectors and artists to pay tax debts by donating significant artworks. The collection includes works by famous artists like Diego Rivera, Frida Kahlo, and Rufino Tamayo as well as many cutting-edge contemporary works.

voyage.name: Museo Vivo del Muralismo
voyage.alt: formerly Secretaría de Educación Pública/Ministry of Public Education
voyage.content: This museum is housed in a former convent from 1729 that later became headquarters for the Education Secretariat. In 1923, the department commissioned the up-and-coming Diego Rivera to decorate the building with 124 mural panels, extending over two city blocks and filling three levels. There are elaborate panels of traditional Mexican life on the ground floor, state seals on the second floor, and themes of revolution

voyage.name: Museo de la Ciudad de México
voyage.alt: Museum of the City of Mexico
voyage.price: M$29 (adults), M$14.50 (students/teachers/INAPAM members); free on W
voyage.content: This museum presents the history of the city in an 18th-century mansion; the building is possibly more interesting than the contents. It is believed that a conquistador's house used to be on the site, as evidenced by the southwest cornerstone of an Aztec serpent head likely taken from the Templo Mayor.

voyage.name: Memorial del 68
voyage.price: M$30 (adults), M$15 (students), free (children under 6); free admission on Su
voyage.content: In UNAM's University Cultural Center Tlatelolco (CCUT) at the Plaza de las Tres Culturas (see Landmarks, above), Memorial 68 is a well-put together museum chronicling the events surrounding the police massacre of student protesters at Tlatelolco in 1968, around the time of the Summer Olympics, which were hosted in Mexico City that year. It's definitely worth a look, but all explanatory text and video interviews are i

voyage.name: Museo Memoria y Tolerancia
voyage.price: M$75 (adults), M$60 (students/teachers/seniors); temporary exhibits: M$30 (adults), M$15 (concessions)
voyage.hours: Tue-Fri 09:00-18:00, Sat Sun 10:00-19:00; last tickets sold ½ hr before closing
voyage.content: Opened in 2010, this museum is dedicated to the remembrance of genocides and crimes against humanity committed around the globe, with the goal of promoting peace and tolerance. Separate sections of the museum are devoted to the Holocaust, Bosnia-Herzegovina, Rwanda, the Khmer Rouge, Darfur, Armenia, and Guatemala. Genocide is only one of the issues the museum confronts. Exhibits also explore hate crimes committed in

voyage.name: Museo de la Indumentaria Mexicana
voyage.content: Collection of traditional Mexican clothing.

voyage.name: Museo del Calzado El Borceguí
voyage.content: Private collection of old shoes from the 18th, 19th and 20th centuries. The museum belongs to the shoe store El Borcegui, established in 1865 and still selling shoes today.

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de las Culturas
voyage.content: Housed in the former Mint building built in 1734. The museum is dedicated to anthropology of the world.

voyage.name: Museo Archivo de la Fotografia
voyage.content: Housed in the historic 16th-century Casa de las Ajaracas, it is a rare survivor on a street that has seen other historic structures knocked down to explore the Templo Mayor site. The museum is home to a huge collection of historical photographs from the 19th, 20th and 21st centuries, documenting the constantly changing cityscape of Mexico City.

voyage.name: Centro Cultural de España en México
voyage.alt: CCEMx / Cultural Center of Spain in Mexico
voyage.content: This is the official cultural center from the Spanish Embassy and features temporary exhibits.

voyage.name: Museo de San Ildefonso
voyage.alt: Antiguo Colegio de San Ildefonso / San Ildefonso College
voyage.price: M$50 (adults), M$25 (students/teachers), free (children under 12); free admission on Tu
voyage.content: Managed by the National University, this museum features some stunning murals and hosts great permanent and temporary art exhibits.

voyage.name: Museo del Estanquillo
voyage.content: One of the newest museums in the city, this contains the personal collection of paintings, photography, and books of the Mexican journalist and writer Carlos Monsivais.

voyage.name: Museo de la Caricatura
voyage.content: Depicting the history of Mexican cartoons (political and amusing cartoons).

voyage.name: Museo de la Luz
voyage.content: Managed by the National University, this museum is mostly for students on everything to do with light (photography, electricity, vision, etc).

voyage.name: Museo de la Charrería
voyage.alt: Ex Templo de Nuestra Señora de Montserrat
voyage.content: This museum features everything about the Mexican Cowboy, known as Charro.

voyage.name: Museo Legislativo
voyage.address: Honorable Congreso de la Unión #66, Col. Delegacion
voyage.content: Museum dedicated to Mexico's Congress, with exhibits about the legislative process and the two houses: the Senate and the Chamber of Deputies. The building houses the legislative chamber of the larger house (Chamber of Deputies). The Senate conducts sessions in a different building on Av. Reforma. Congressional tours are conducted through the museum and include the opportunity to enter the Chamber of Deputies. This b

voyage.name: Centro de la Imagen
voyage.content: This is one of Mexico City's premier exhibition spaces for photography, with rotating exhibits of work by Mexican and international photographers. The center also has a small bookstore.

voyage.name: Palacio de Iturbide
voyage.alt: Palacio de Cultura Banamex / Palace of Iturbide
voyage.content: One of the oldest buildings in town, built in the late 16th century, it was first home to the local nobility and later the residence of Mexican Emperor Agustin de Iturbide. The building is owned today by the Cultural Trust of Banco Nacional de Mexico, the Mexican branch of Citibank.

voyage.name: Palacio de Bellas Artes
voyage.price: Free (lobby), M$60 for mezzanine with murals and galleries; $M30 photography permit; free admission on Sundays
voyage.hours: Tue-Sun 10:00-18:00; last admission ½ hr before closing
voyage.content: Designed by Italian architect Adamo Boari. Construction started in 1905, however due to the Revolution War, it was not completed until 1934. The building is so heavy that it has sunk 4½m into the former lakebed. It is considered to be one of the best examples of Mexican Art Deco architecture; architectural and interior features include its copper cupolas and a Tiffany stained-glass stage curtain designed by Mexican p

voyage.name: Palacio Postal
voyage.content: One of the most beautiful buildings in the country and considered a National Heritage Building. Built in 1906, this European style building houses the main post office. Most of the materials used to build it were brought from Italy.

voyage.name: Museo Postal
voyage.content: Housed in the Postal Palace, features old postal stationery and mail boxes.

voyage.name: Banco de México
voyage.address: Cinco de Mayo and Avda Eje Central
voyage.content: Office of the Mexican Central Bank, built in 1925.

voyage.name: Casa Rivas Mercado
voyage.content: Architecturally unique and utterly fascinating restored neoclassical mansion from the Porfiriato era of the 19th century with period furnishings. Guided tours (in Spanish).

voyage.name: Torre Latinoamericana
voyage.content: Construction started in 1948 and was completed in 1956. This was Mexico's first skyscraper, boasting 44 floors and 182 meters. There is an observatory in the 42nd floor.

voyage.name: Biblioteca Miguel Lerdo de Tejada
voyage.alt: Library of Miguel Lerdo de Tejada
voyage.content: This Baroque building was built as a church, but in the 1960s was repurposed to house a library. For visitors the primary interest is a series of enormous murals painted by the Russian emigré painter Vladimir Kibalchich Russakov (known in Mexico simply as Vlady). The murals in the main room are titled La Revolución y los Elementos (or 'Revolution and the Elements'). They required eight years to complete and are consi

voyage.name: Biblioteca de México José Vasconcelos
voyage.content: Located in a former tobacco factory, it is one of the largest libraries in the city. It contains several beautiful courtyards and smaller libraries decorated according to the character of different Mexican authors who donated their book collections to the library.

voyage.name: Biblioteca Vasconcelos
voyage.content: Next to Buenavista train station, it is the largest library in Mexico and functions as a central library for other libraries in the country. It is housed in an impressive modern building designed by architects Alberto Kalach and Juan Palomar. It is a must for visitors with an interest in architecture, not only for its stunning exterior design, but for its famous "floating stacks" that create the illusion of book shel

voyage.name: Colonia Santa María la Ribera
voyage.content: A colonia in the Cuauhtémoc borough, 2 km west of the historic center. This area was designated as a "Barrio Mágico" by the city in 2011. It was created in the late 19th century and reached its height between 1910 and 1930. In the 1930s, the middle class moved in and a new era of construction began. Today, the colonia is a mix of old mansions and homes (with over 1,000 categorized has having architectural or historic

voyage.name: Alameda de Santa María la Ribera
voyage.content: This historic park, established in 1861, is the heart of Santa María la Ribera. Its centerpiece is the Kiosco Morisco, an Art Nouveau pavilion built in 1884 for the New Orleans World’s Fair and relocated here in 1910. Surrounded by jacaranda trees and tiled fountains, it hosts dance classes, markets, and music on weekends.

voyage.name: Museo del Instituto de Geología de la UNAM
voyage.content: Housed in a 1906 Porfirian building in Santa María la Ribera, this museum showcases Mexico’s geological heritage with a mammoth skeleton, the dinosaur Isauria, and extensive mineral and fossil collections. Interactive exhibits and José María Velasco’s paintings enhance the experience.

voyage.name: Parroquia Josefina de la Sagrada Familia
voyage.content: This late 19th-century Byzantine-style church in Santa María la Ribera, designed by Carlos Herrera, is a hidden gem. Its vibrant interior features murals by Pedro Cruz depicting the life of St. Joseph, Christ’s birth, and the flight to Egypt, alongside stunning stained-glass windows and unique woodwork. A serene space for reflection, it’s a cultural treasure in one of Mexico City’s historic neighborhoods.

voyage.name: Museo Universitario del Chopo
voyage.content: Housed in a striking 1902 iron-and-glass building by Enrique Norten, this UNAM-managed museum in Santa María la Ribera focuses on contemporary art. It features rotating exhibits of avant-garde works, performances, and workshops. A cultural hub with a modernist vibe.

voyage.name: Colonia Tabaclera
voyage.content: A colonia in the Cuauhtémoc borough of Mexico City, on the western edge of the Centro Histórico and the Zona Rosa. This area was developed in the early 1900s with a mix of mansions and upscale apartment buildings, but its fortunes had declined by the end of the 20th century and the area is a bit rough at night with seedy characters engaged in prostitution, drug dealing, and petty crime, though it is generally safe du

voyage.name: Teatro de la Ciudad
voyage.content: Historic theatre that was built to resemble La Scala in Milan. It is a huge theatre with stacks of balcony levels looking onto the stage below. The best seats are on the 1st balcony level (better than main level seats). The theatre hosts a range of performances, many plays, but also dance, music, and other forms.

voyage.name: Balet Folklorico
voyage.content: Iconic performances of regional traditional dance and music from all parts of Mexico. The performance hall itself is a spectacular example of Art Deco architecture and features a stained glass curtain designed by famed muralist Dr. Atl.

voyage.name: Arena Coliseo
voyage.content: A famous venue for lucha libre (Mexican wrestling) and boxing.

voyage.name: Mercado de la Merced
voyage.address: bounded by Santa Escuela, General Anaya, Rosario, and Cerrado del Rosario
voyage.content: One of the largest and most famous markets in Mexico, La Merced was built in 1860 and covers several blocks with tianguis style vendors lining nearby streets. The market mainly sells food and household items; if you're looking to cook for yourself or just want to wander aisles of stalls selling cheap limes or huitlacoche, this is the place to go. Many vendors offer tastings. Foreigners will stick out a bit, but not e

voyage.name: Mercado de Sonora
voyage.address: Av Fray Servando Teresa de Mier
voyage.content: One of the more interesting markets, this specializes in traditional medicines, as well as paraphernalia for Santa Muerte and voodoo. Endangered animals are also sold here, and the market is regularly raided by the police. The area is not as safe as the higher-class neighborhoods to the west; exercise caution.

voyage.name: Mercado de San Juan
voyage.content: This market specializing in gourmet foods, and is frequented by many of Mexico City's top chefs. On offer are many foods imported from Europe and elsewhere, including such specialties as European cheeses, Spanish and Italian sausage, pre-Hispanic foods and exotic meats.

voyage.name: Mercado de Artesanías de San Juan
voyage.alt: San Juan Arts and Crafts Market
voyage.content: Vendors here sell a full range of Mexican handicrafts from across the country, including pottery, textiles, carving, leatherwork, and jewelry.

voyage.name: Mercado de la Ciudadela
voyage.content: Tourist-oriented handicrafts market with over 350 vendors from all over Mexico, first established for the 1968 Olympics. Cleaner and more expensive than the other markets in the city.

voyage.name: Mercado Lagunilla
voyage.address: Prolongación Paseo de la Reforma and Francisco Bocanegra
voyage.content: This huge street market features antiques and other new goods such as clothing, crafts, food, jewelry and toys. It is considered safe to stroll in this street market, but try to remain in the streets near Francisco Bocanegra and Comonfor, because beyond that the market eventually blends into Tepito, another market which is a lot less safe.

voyage.name: Tianguis Cultural del Chopo
voyage.content: Huge outdoor flea market. Focuses on alternative music including grunge, heavy metal, punk and ska. Bands play at one end of the park.

voyage.name: Pino Suarez
voyage.content: There is a lot of youth-minded fashion going on here. Most of it is a knock-off of something else but at such low prices who can complain? There is a very large indoor market near the metro stop that has a ton of clothing, shoes, and food vendors.

voyage.name: Avenida de República de Salvador
voyage.content: The first half of the street (from Avenida Eje Central Avenue to Avenida Isabel la Católica) specializes in all sorts of electronics. From spare parts (speakers, wiring, transistors) to complete home theater systems, audio mixers and lighting for dance clubs. The other half of the street (from Isabel la Católica) specializes in stationery and paper.

voyage.name: Avenida Eje Central
voyage.content: This street is full of street vendors. The area is extremely crowded making it a paradise for pickpockets.

voyage.name: Fan Center
voyage.content: Seven floors of nerd culture stores selling video games and collectibles.

voyage.name: Frikiplaza
voyage.content: Four floors of nerd culture stores selling video games and collectibles.

voyage.name: Calle del Artículo 123
voyage.content: Specializes in appliances, from spare parts to industrial vacuums and blenders.

voyage.name: Calle Victoria
voyage.content: Specializes in lighting, from wiring and electric outlets to chandeliers and lamps.

voyage.name: Calle de Donceles
voyage.content: Specializes in photography.

voyage.name: Calle de República de Cuba
voyage.content: Specializes in printing (books, posters, thesis). In this street there are a few book stores selling very old books (18th and 19th centuries).

voyage.name: Barrio Chino
voyage.content: Two pedestrian-only blocks of this street, where much of the city's Chinese community lived in the early 1900s, are full of Chinese restaurants and stores.

voyage.name: Calle Tacuba
voyage.content: Eyeglasses, contact lenses, and dozens of opticians.

voyage.name: Liverpool
voyage.content: This department store is housed in an Art-Deco building that was built in the late 1920s.

voyage.name: El Palacio de Hierro
voyage.content: This department store was established in 1891. The store was named when it was the first iron and steel building in the city.

voyage.name: Sanborns
voyage.content: This department store and restaurant is housed in the former residency of the Counts of the Valley of Orizaba. Revolutionist Emiliano Zapata had breakfast here during his entrance to Mexico City in September 1916. This was the first store of the Mexican Sanborns chain, founded by the Sanborn brothers, American immigrants in Mexico City and later sold to Walgreens in 1946 and then to Grupo Carso in 1985. There are mor

voyage.name: Sanborns
voyage.content: This department store is housed in a building completed in 1900 named 'Casa Boker' after a warehouse store with that name that still occupies part of the building.

voyage.name: El Nuevo Mundo
voyage.content: Still contains old fashioned practices such as old-style shopping processes. When decide to buying something, the salesman will prepare a small receipt, then you take it to the cashier to pay.

voyage.name: C&A
voyage.content: Netherlands-based department store fashion retailer.

voyage.name: Pastelería Ideal
voyage.content: Established in 1927. This is a good place for traditional bread, pastries and desserts. Ask for Danes de Chocolate, the place's delicacy. There is another branch at Av 16 de Septiembre 18 which makes cakes on commission.

voyage.name: Pasteleria Madrid
voyage.content: This is a very old and typical bakery, they will usually have fresh bread twice a day, but if there are a lot of customers they will bake as many as four times a day. Also serves breakfast platters, pastries and pan dulce.

voyage.name: Forum Buenavista
voyage.content: The largest shopping mall close to the centro. Includes a large supermarket, a Sears department store, and a Cinepolis cinema complex. This mall is inside the Buenavista train station, which has frequent train service provided by Ferrocarril Suburbano as well as three Metro subway lines and numerous Metrobus connections.

voyage.name: Patio Juárez
voyage.content: A small shopping mall.

voyage.name: Street food alley
voyage.content: There is a big variety of street food.

voyage.name: Food stall market
voyage.content: At different times there are other food stalls open.

voyage.name: Cocuyo's
voyage.hours: Daily 08:00 - 05:00 (yes, they only close for 3 hours)
voyage.content: One of Mexico City's many famous taco stands, Cocuyo's has been featured on international food shows including Anthony Bourdain's No Reservations and the Netflix series, Taco Chronicles. The place has changed since Bourdain visited. They now have a dining room so you no longer have to stand on the street while you eat your taco, but the tacos are big and tasty as ever and they're still open in the wee hours of the ni

voyage.name: Mercado San Juan Arcos de Belen
voyage.content: It is full of food stalls offering all the Mexican favorites. Find the one opposite the small bakers by one of the rear entrances on Calle Delicias, which serves the Torta Cubana. The people running it are amazingly welcoming and the food, especially the Cubana, is excellent.

voyage.name: Don Toribio
voyage.content: Delicious traditional Mexican cuisine at some of the best prices in Centro.

voyage.name: Roldan 37
voyage.content: Cozy upstairs restaurant specializing in chiles rellenos, including the national dish of chile en nogada. Very authentic cooking with several regional dishes based on indigenous traditions, and sometimes unusual ingredients that will offend the tastes of unsuspecting foreigners who might not appreciate the chance to eat grasshoppers. Though rest assured, there are plenty of "normal" dishes to choose from.

voyage.name: Cafe el Popular
voyage.content: Long-time fixture in the heart of downtown. Traditional homemade Mexican food including fresh baked breads, though the restaurant is historically Chinese and once served hybrid Mexicanized Chinese dishes. The place is known for its coffee and of course is a dependable source of good, hearty food when the midnight munchies strike.

voyage.name: Chung King
voyage.content: Generous plates, many of which are ramen. Spicy red chili sauce is provided for people who want to take the flavor up a notch.

voyage.name: Kang Qing
voyage.content: Buffet style restaurant with to-go service at 65 pesos, making it very cheap for a lot of food.

voyage.name: Bufet Comida China
voyage.content: Chinese buffet serving lots of food at low prices.

voyage.name: El Huequito Bolivar
voyage.content: This taco joint is good if you want to try tacos al pastor, as featured in Anthony Bourdain's Mexico show.

voyage.name: Cafeteria El Cuadrilatero
voyage.content: This torteria is owned by former luchador Super Astro, and serves not only tortas but also standard Mexican fare. Their enormous torta Super Gladiator is free if you can eat the whole thing in 15 minutes.

voyage.name: La Opera Bar
voyage.content: This restaurant has been serving Mexican food since the early 1900s and retains the same furniture since then. When you get there, look up to the ceiling, as you will see the famous gun shot accidentally fired by Pancho Villa.

voyage.name: El Ehden
voyage.content: This restaurant is favored by the local Mexican-Lebanese community, many of whom still own the small businesses and textile shops in the immediate area. It serves a range of standard Lebanese dishes, including an excellent mezze.

voyage.name: El Mayor
voyage.content: A newer rooftop establishment with great seating overlooking the Templo Mayor, this restaurant specializes in creative twists to traditional Mexican dishes. It's very popular for lunch, so it's best to arrive early.

voyage.name: Hostería de Santo Domingo
voyage.content: Housed in a former inn, this restaurant opened in 1860 and is the oldest restaurant in Mexico City. It serves classic traditional Mexican dishes in a lively atmosphere, and is very popular with residents.

voyage.name: El Cardenal
voyage.content: Upscale dining room serving outstanding regional and traditional Mexican cuisine. The restaurant has been a favorite of businessmen and politicos for generations. The food is always excellent, as is the service. They bake their own breads, offer several moles, offer unusual entrees, and are famous for their hot chocolate. Can be crowded weekdays for lunch and Sunday mornings. This listing is near the Zócalo, other lo

voyage.name: Dulcería de Celaya
voyage.content: This confectionery shop sells old fashioned sweets. It was established in 1874 and still has its original cabinets from that age.

voyage.name: Limosneros
voyage.content: Elegantly rustic dining room with innovative regional cuisine and a full bar with a variety of mezcals, tequilas, and an excellent wine list featuring many great Baja vintages. Adventurous palates shouild try the carnitas de conejo.

voyage.name: Paxia
voyage.content: Elegant rooftop restaurant with innovative nuevo Mexican cuisine and spectacular views of the historic downtown area.

voyage.name: Testal
voyage.content: Trendy casual restaurant serving traditional Mexican and regional dishes. Great breakfast and interesting dishes at lunch and dinner including nogales en chile, mole and more. Family friendly with affordable prices.

voyage.name: Café de Tacuba
voyage.content: Housed in a former convent, this institution serves up tasty Mexican dishes all day for reasonable prices. It is very popular so arrive early. Menu is in English and Spanish.

voyage.name: La Terraza
voyage.content: Restaurant on the roof of the Hotel Majestic overlooking the Zócalo, with stunning panoramic views of the city.

voyage.name: Los Girasoles
voyage.content: Traditional Mexican cuisine from various regions. Expect dishes like mole oaxqueno and if you're adventurous, chapulines. Pleasant outdoor patio on a plaza made for people watching. Mariachis on weekends.

voyage.name: Miralto
voyage.content: Many places in the Centro Histórico boast of the views from their rooftop dining rooms, but Miralto in the 41st floor of the Torre Latinoamericana looks down on all of them. Best views of any dining room in the city. Traditional Mexican cuisine is good, but unexceptional compared to the city's top restaurants.

voyage.name: Azul Histórico
voyage.content: Azul offers upscale Mexican cuisine in a romantic Centro courtyard with lush trees and stone archways.

voyage.name: Masala y Maiz
voyage.content: Elegant restaurant serving a fusion of contemporary Mexican cuisine with flavors and ingredients from Africa and India. Dishes are often unusual combinations like a paratha quesadilla, or a chai tres leches. Service is top notch. Reservations recommended. The restaurant was awarded a Michelin star in 2025.

voyage.name: Balcon del Zocalo
voyage.content: Rooftop dining atop the Hotel Zocalo Central. Food is nouveau Mexican with a number of unusual and creative fusions. The 9-course tasting menu is recommended because it highlights small plates showcasing various chef selections. The views are the best in the city with the Catedral Metropolitano and the Palacio Nacional lying just below (the night views make great photos with everything lit up). Very tourist friendly

voyage.name: Salón Tenampa
voyage.content: The original and most famous Mexican cantina, traditional home to the bohemians and mariachis of the 40s and 50s. Huge selection of tequila and mezcal, light Mexican food, and mariachi bands.

voyage.name: La Opera
voyage.content: Traditional bar dating back to the Porfiriato era (est. 1870), it's ornate and impressive to see, but a fun place to have a beer or a cocktail. Serves food.

voyage.name: Salón España
voyage.content: Old school traditional cantina where the tequila is strong and the men drink lots of it. They have mezcal and other liquors as well, but tequila is king here with more than 150 brands at your call! Free botanas (including tacos and quesadillas) while you continue drinking.

voyage.name: Bar La Giaconda
voyage.content: Casual place with good baguette sandwiches and dark draft beer.

voyage.name: Sunday Sunday
voyage.content: While the lightweights are nursing their hangovers on Sunday, the hardcore head to Mexico City's biggest Sunday night party where the house keeps rocking until 2am. The biggest crowds hit after midnight.

voyage.name: Salon Corona
voyage.content: Friendly traditional cantina since 1928. Popular place to watch a soccer game or hang out and drink beer. Serves traditional Mexican food.

voyage.name: La Faena
voyage.hours: Mon-Fri 13:00 - 20:00, Fri-Sat 13:00 - 10:30 (yep, they close for 2-1/2 hours to clean up)
voyage.content: Old school cantina that celebrates the hispanic tradition of bullfighting. Campy wall decorations, a great jukebox full of classic Mexican rancheras, rock en espanol, and pop hits of the 90s. Cheap tacos, great variety of mezcal and tequila drinks, and a very lively crowd.

voyage.name: Bosforo
voyage.content: Dim, smoky bar with a hipster crowd. No sign, so you need to know where it is then look for the curtain across the doorway. Go in and join the crowd in sampling one of the city's widest selection of mezcals.

voyage.name: Cantina Tio Pepe
voyage.content: Traditional cantina with an early 20th-century vibe. Friendly atmosphere, occasional mariachis.

voyage.name: Pulquería Las Duelistas
voyage.content: Friendly and colorful traditional pulqueria (one of the most popular in the city) with murals on the ceiling and walls. Serves cured and white (blanco) pulques. Try a natural pulque to taste pure agave flavor, or try one of the fruit or spiced flavors. The celery (apio) is recommended.

voyage.name: La Joya
voyage.address: Eligio Ancona 122, Santa Maria La Ribera
voyage.content: This used to be the Xochitl Pulqueria, but it changed hands in 2020 while keeping the tacky decor and the limited menu of just the pulques, only the pulques, and nothing but pulques, so help me God. Natural and curadas are available with flavors that include spices, fruits, and nuts.

voyage.name: Marrakech Salon
voyage.content: Wonderfully tacky flaming gay bar with drag queens and strippers for entertainment, no cover charge for anyone, and some delicious house mezcal drinks. Try the El Mayate --- minty and refreshing!

voyage.name: La Purisima
voyage.content: Delightfully tacky strip shows and disco balls. Very friendly crowd.

voyage.name: Cafe Equis
voyage.content: In business at the same location since 1930, this is Mexico City's oldest coffee house. They roast their own beans, specializing in organic Mexican-grown coffees. Cups of joe are also available for as little as M$15. The Cafe Veracruzano is sinfully delicious with a flavor of caramelized burnt sugar. Cash only.

voyage.name: Cafe Regina
voyage.content: Good coffee drinks plus hot chocolate and tea. Light food available including baked goods and vegetarian dishes like ratatouille.

voyage.name: Café La Habana
voyage.price: M$69–140 for breakfast packages, coffee from M$30
voyage.content: Opened in 1952, this iconic café is a nostalgic gem, steeped in history as a meeting place for revolutionaries like Fidel Castro and Che Guevara, who reportedly planned the Cuban Revolution here, and literary giants like Gabriel García Márquez and Roberto Bolaño, who frequented it during the 1970s infrarrealist movement. With its high ceilings, sepia-toned photos of Havana, and vintage coffee machine, it retains a 19

voyage.name: Hotel San Francisco
voyage.content: Sparsely furnished, inexpensive rooms.

voyage.name: Hotel Tuxpan
voyage.content: A very good deal. Clean with cable TV, nice restrooms, and mirrors on the ceiling.

voyage.name: Mexico City Hostel
voyage.content: Breakfast included, Internet, laundry, lockers, tours and tourist information.

voyage.name: Casa de los Amigos
voyage.content: Established in the 1950s by the Quaker community in Mexico City, the Casa continues to be actively involved in local activities with a stated mission of promoting peace and international understanding. They run an affordable guest house (with either private rooms or dorm beds) with a two-night minimum, and is popular with international students or volunteers on extended stays, though there are still many who are "jus

voyage.name: Hostel Mundo Joven Catedral
voyage.content: A clean and safe upscale hostel. Some rooms have partial views of the rear of the cathedral, but these are noisy due to the church bells. Discount with a Hosteling International card.

voyage.name: Hotel Juarez
voyage.content: A well taken care of hotel. Large rooms, TV, phone (free local calls) and private bathroom. Rooms may not all have windows.

voyage.name: Hotel Principal
voyage.content: Clean, friendly, and well run hotel with a range of rooms. Most overlook a quiet inner courtyard.

voyage.name: Cadillac Hotel Boutique
voyage.content: Stylish artsy place, very modern with excellent free breakfast. No A/C so better choice for winter than summer.

voyage.name: Hotel Metropol
voyage.content: Dated hotel that could use some redecorating tips, but rooms are spacious, they serve a buffet breakfast.

voyage.name: Gran Hotel Ciudad de México
voyage.content: This building built in 1899 was once a luxurious shopping center. It was converted into a hotel in 1966. The lobby of this place was featured in the film Frida.

voyage.name: Best Western Hotel Majestic
voyage.content: The location is great, the rooms are clean and comfortable but the service is vaudevillian. The restaurant on the top floor has a superb view of the Cathedral and Presidential Palace but the food isn't worthy of the atmosphere.

voyage.name: Castillo de Chapultepec y Museo Nacional de Historia (MNH)
voyage.price: Adult M$210, Mexican citizens and residents M$105 (ID required); seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays for Mexican citizens and residents; video camera and flash photography is not permitted
voyage.content: The imposing castle on top of the hill calls to visitors. Over its history, it has been the home of the Spanish Viceroys, a military college, a scene of historic battle during the Mexican-American War, the palace of Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlotta, the national observatory, and the presidential palace. It is now a museum. You can walk about 1 km up the winding hill road, or take the tram that departs every tw

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Arte Moderno
voyage.content: It showcases temporary exhibitions of Mexican and international art, and has a permanent collection of work by artists including Frida Kahlo, Diego Rivera, David Siqueiros, José Orozco, and Leonora Carrington, among others.

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Antropología
voyage.price: Adult M$210, Mexican citizens and residents M$105 (ID required); seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays for Mexican citizens and residents
voyage.address: Av Paseo de la Reforma y Calzada Gandhi s/n
voyage.content: One of the top anthropology museums in the world. This enormous complex highlights the development and cultures of Mexico's many indigenous peoples from thousands of years ago to today, and is full to the brim with ancient artifacts and artwork. Also, the museum itself is famous for its architecture. It is possible to spend days here to see everything – allocate two hours at the very least, prioritize your specific i

voyage.name: Museo Rufino Tamayo
voyage.price: Adult M$95; seniors over 60, children under 13, teachers: free; free on Sundays
voyage.content: The original collection of this modern art museum was donated by the late Oaxacan-Zapoteca artist Rufino Tamayo and his wife, and includes works by Picasso, Rothko, and Miró, Georgia O'Keefe and many others. The collection also includes works from pre-Hispanic civilizations and works by Tamayo himself. Tamayo was heavily influenced by pre-Hispanic cultures, as were other modern artists in Mexico during the 20th centu

voyage.name: Sala de Arte Publico Siqueiros
voyage.price: M$12 adults; free for students, teachers, seniors, children under 12; free admission on Sundays
voyage.content: This museum showcases the works of famed Mexican muralist David Alfaro Siquerios.

voyage.name: Zoologico de Chapultepec
voyage.price: Free except for the butterfly or reptile houses
voyage.content: Large, modern zoo in the same style as major ones in the U.S., famous for its pandas. Very crowded on weekends. Highlights for foreign visitors are the Anfibium axolotl center showcasing the unique endangered salamanders native to Mexico City, and the tropical forests section which is relatively uncrowded and has a large proportion of animals native to Mexico and Central America, like jaguars, spider monkeys, and tap

voyage.name: ANFIBIUM: Museo del Axolote y Centro de Conservación de Anfibios
voyage.alt: Museum of the Axolotl and Amphibian Conservation Center
voyage.content: Located inside the zoo, but an attraction of its own, this popular facility exhibits the axolotl, Mexico City's unusual native salamander species, which reproduces without ever reaching adulthood and can re-grow almost any part of its body, but is now almost extinct in the wild. On the first floor you can see the axolotls and several related species in naturalistic enclosures, and on the second floor you can see the

voyage.name: Monumento a los Niños Héroes
voyage.content: This impressive white marble monument stands at the entrance to Chapultepec Park in front of the Castillo. It honors six youths who gave their lives defending the stronghold from US troops in 1847. In the most dramatic telling of the legend, a cadet jumped to his death wrapped in the Mexican flag rather than surrendering to the American troops.

voyage.name: Casa Gilardi
voyage.content: Outstanding house tour that will appeal to anyone interested in modern architecture. The house was designed by world famous architect Luis Barragan (whose nearby home and studio is a ). Casa Gilardi is one of Barragan's signature projects, a private home that incorporates his concepts of human livability, integration with nature, and his bold use of brilliant colors and juxtaposed shapes. Reservations must be made in

voyage.name: Baths of Moctezuma
voyage.content: A system of tanks, reservoirs, canals and waterfalls constructed by the Aztecs.

voyage.name: Museo de Historia Natural y Cultura Ambiental
voyage.price: M$23 adults; M$11 teachers, students, children 3-12; free for seniors, disabled, children under 3; free admission on Tuesday
voyage.address: Bosque de Chapultepec II, Circuíto Correr es Salud s/n
voyage.content: Exhibits a history of evolution, with dinosaurs, whales, viruses, bugs, plants, human organs and more. If it's natural, it's here.

voyage.name: Luis Barragán House and Studio
voyage.price: M$400 adults, M$300 Mexican citizens, M$200 students
voyage.address: Gral. Francisco Ramírez 12, Ampliación Daniel Garza, Miguel Hidalgo, CDMX
voyage.content: The home and studio of the famed Mexican architect Luis Barragán has been turned into a museum dedicated to his life and work. The house looks plain from the outside, but inside it opens up and exemplifies Barragan's modernist design philosophy of integrating light, and nature with open, aesthetically pleasing spaces and surfaces to create a serene and functional living space for humans. It is a .

voyage.name: Panteon Civil de Dolores
voyage.content: Largest cemetery in Mexico, site of the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons. The cemetery has over 1 million grave sites. People are just dying to get in here!

voyage.name: Museo del Dolores de Cárcamo
voyage.address: Av. Rodolfo Neri Vela, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc
voyage.content: Small museum housed in a historic waterworks building, it houses a famous mural by Diego Rivera that could be considered a work of sculpture because part of it is a 3-dimensional bust while part of it is a tile mosaic mural covered by water.

voyage.name: Los Pinos
voyage.address: Calz. del Rey S/N, Bosque de Chapultepec I Secc
voyage.content: Mexico's "White House", which isn't white, but is the official residence of recent presidents. Since Andres Lopez Obrador was elected president in 2018, he and his successor have chosen to live in the Capitol building (Palacio Nacional), believing Los Pinos to be too opulent for a Mexican public servant. That decision leaves the official residence and grounds open for public tours and cultural events. Los Pinos is ac

voyage.name: Papalote Childrens Museum
voyage.content: Cutting edge hands-on childrens activities to nurture young minds

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Energía y Tecnología
voyage.address: Av. de los Compositores s/n, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc
voyage.content: Planes, trains and automobiles. Pretty much any other kind of machine too, from steam engines of the industrial age to AI and the robotics of tomorrow. Great place for teens!

voyage.name: Ex-Fabrica de Polvora
voyage.content: Built by the Spanish military at the end of the colonial era; it is now used for cultural exhibits.

voyage.name: Lago de Chapultepec
voyage.content: There are actually two lakes that are connected, a bridge spanning them at mid-point. Lounge around the shore, or rent a canoe or paddleboat to explore.

voyage.name: Lanchacinema
voyage.content: A large movie screen is set up on the shore of Lake Chapultepec and movie goers sit in paddle boats in the lake to watch the movies. The movies are shown on a sporadic schedule, so consult current park info to see if a movie night is taking place during your visit to the city.

voyage.name: Parque Aztlan
voyage.price: Free, fees for each ride vary
voyage.address: Av. de los Compositores s/n, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc
voyage.content: Modern urban theme park opened in 2024. Thrill rides like roller coaster, swing, giant Ferris wheel and more. Requires a rechargeable card to pay for rides, which cost up to M$120 per ride. Restrooms cost M$5 to use (also paid via rechargeable card). Variety of concessions.

voyage.name: Jardín Botánico
voyage.content: 5.3 hectare garden showcasing more than 300 species of native Mexican plant life.

voyage.name: Pista el Sope
voyage.content: Wide running tracks and trails with mixed elevations. Groomed, chipped clay surface. Warm up area. Very popular among local runners and fitness enthusiasts.

voyage.name: Auditorio Nacional
voyage.content: Venue for performing arts and popular entertainers. Shows include family friendly events like the Nutcracker Suite, Placido Domingo, and Disney on Ice as well as popular Latin and international performers including Chayanne and Gilberto Santa Rosa. Seats 10,000. Tickets available through TicketMaster.

voyage.name: Campo Marte
voyage.content: Officially a military sports field owned by the Ministry of Defense (SEDENA), this is a well-known polo field where prestigious international matches have taken place, including the World Polo Championship in 2008 and the Prince of Wales Cup in 1993 (attended by Prince Charles, now King Charles). The regular polo season runs from November through April. Information about polo events and teams is available through the

voyage.name: Mercado el Chorrito
voyage.content: Large public market, lots of food vendors. Local vibe, not tourist oriented.

voyage.name: Bistro Chapultepec
voyage.address: Lago Mayor, Secc. II, Bosque de Chapultepec
voyage.content: Elegant lakeside dining in Chapultepec park, outdoor dining area available. Menu is more American or European than Mexican, which may appeal to some travelers. Reservations accepted.

voyage.name: Del Bosque
voyage.address: Lago Menor, Del Rosal s/n, Bosque De Chapultepec
voyage.content: Casual upscale dining with traditional Mexican cuisine. The restaurant is in Chapultepec Park, with a lakeside setting. The dining rooms features a glass wall with views of the lake right outside the restaurant.

voyage.name: City Café Natural El Sope
voyage.address: Av. de los Corredores S/N, Sección II, Bosque de Chapultepec
voyage.content: Casual outdoor cafe specializing in coffee and breakfast. Popular with runners and dog walkers alike. Very pet friendly with an area set aside for customers with well-behaved, leashed dogs.

voyage.name: Lago/Algo
voyage.address: Bosque de Chapultepec, Pista El Sope S/N, Bosque de Chapultepec II Secc
voyage.content: Sophisticated upscale dining in a landmark of modern architecture built on the edge of one of the lakes in Chapultepec Park. A cross between elegant dining and a cultural center that includes a gallery of contemporary art and spaces for cultural events. The menu is contemporary international cuisine with European favorites and seafood specialties that are less common in Mexico (like mussels). Tables can be reserved o

voyage.name: Alfredo di Roma
voyage.content: This is a charming and luxurious restaurant which serves slightly expensive Italian fare that is surprisingly worth it. Be sure to try the Fettuccine Alfredo or the Torre de Pisa, which is mouth-wateringly delicious.

voyage.name: Comal Oculto
voyage.content: Small traditional restaurant serving antojitos and other light fare. The house specialty is roasted pork shoulder tacos.

voyage.name: Mari Gold
voyage.address: Calle Gob.Protasio Tagle 66A, San Miguel Chapultepec II Secc
voyage.content: Deliciously fascinating fusion of nouveau Mexican cuisine and Indian cuisine served in an elegantly sparse contemporary dining room. While the sabudana vada is recommended, most dishes will be unfamiliar to diners so a wise approach is to talk to the staff and trust in their recommendations.

voyage.name: La Milla
voyage.address: Calle Gral. Fco. Molinos del Campo 19
voyage.content: Small streetside cafe with a few tables outside on the sidewalk and more upstairs on a 2nd floor balcony. Wide range of pastries and baked goods, including several options for vegans. Excellent coffee.

voyage.name: Fiesta Americana Grand Chapultepec
voyage.content: Rooms are clean, quiet and very comfortable.

voyage.name: JW Marriott Mexico City
voyage.content: One of the premier Mexico City hotels, the JW Marriott Hotel Mexico City rises 26 stories high in the exclusive Polanco District. Located in the heart of the business and entertainment sector, this flagship Mexico City hotel is within walking distance to Auditorio Nacional, the city's financial hub, and some of Mexico's best shopping, dining and night life.

voyage.name: Green Park Hotel
voyage.address: Av Costituyentes 99, Col San Miguel Chapultepec,
voyage.content: Comfortable upscale hotel with traditional furnishings. Located adjacent to Chapultepec Park.

voyage.name: Hotel Atlantico
voyage.address: Av Observatorio 218, Daniel Garza al Poniente
voyage.content: Older budget hotel with spacious but minimalist rooms with worn furnishings.

voyage.name: Hotel Park Villa
voyage.address: Calle Gral. Gómez Pedraza 68, San Miguel Chapultepec
voyage.content: Moderate hotel with dated facilities that cry out for renovation and update. Staff are friendly and location is good, across the street from Chapultepec Park and short walk to restaurants and bars of Condesa. Complimentary bicycles.

voyage.name: Hotel Alexander
voyage.address: Bosque de Chapultepec, Lomas - Virreyes, Pedregal 24, Miguel Hidalgo
voyage.content: Modern luxury hotel with spacious, comfortable rooms, well-equipped gym, good breakfast included in rate. First-class service with understated elegance.

voyage.name: Rectoría de la UNAM
voyage.content: For David Alfaro Siqueiros fans, the rectory building is of interest because of its large three-dimensional mosaic mural El pueblo a la Universidad, la Universidad al pueblo (The People to the University, the University to the People), created by the Mexican master from 1952-1956.

voyage.name: Biblioteca Central
voyage.content: The building's four sides are covered by the mural Historical Representation of Culture, created by the Mexican artist Juan O'Gorman. His masterpiece has become the most iconic building of UNAM and of Mexican culture. O'Gorman's mural is recognized as the largest mural in the world.

voyage.name: Museo Universitario de Arte Contemporáneo
voyage.price: M$40 (general admission Th-Sa), M$20 (general admission W and Su), 50% discount for students, free (children under 12)
voyage.content: This museum hosts temporary exhibits of contemporary Mexican and international artists, as well as rotating displays from its permanent art collection.

voyage.name: Jardín Botánico de UNAM
voyage.content: Large botanical garden showcasing thousands of plant species from across Mexico's many different ecosystems, including dry deserts, rocky mountain ranges, tropical and sub-tropical rainforests, and coastal wetlands. The gardens include an extensive collection of cacti. Visitors may be surprised at the extent of the collection (and Mexico's astounding biodiversity - the country is home to more plant and animal species

voyage.name: Estadio Olimpico Universitario
voyage.address: Av. de los Insurgentes Sur S/N, C.U
voyage.content: The stadium actually pre-dates the 1968 Olympics for which it is named. The exterior has a large mural by Diego Rivera titled La Universidad, la familia y el deporte en México; the mural was created between 1952 and 1954. The stadium is used for university athletics and is home field for the Pumas soccer team.

voyage.name: Universum
voyage.content: Comprehensive science and technology museum with exhibits for all ages. Paleontology (dinosaur bones), astronomy (includes a planetarium), chemistry, physics, there are even exhibits that make math look like fun! It's a large museum, so plan to spend most of the day here.

voyage.name: Espacio Escultórico
voyage.address: University Theater Center (CUT), Mario de La Cueva, Cd. Universitaria
voyage.content: Sometimes dubiously described as the world's largest outdoor sculpture, the Espacio Escultórico is a round ring reminiscent of a modernized Stonehenge. It is a wide path lined with angular stone monoliths surrounding a patch of natural volcanic rock.

voyage.name: Museo Universitaria Ciencias y Artes
voyage.content: Open interdisciplinary exhibition space. Typically has an exhibition on a specific topic for a period of a few months, then shuts down until a new exhibition is prepared. (Check the official website for events, other sources are unreliable.)

voyage.name: Museo de Anatomopatolgia Veterinaria
voyage.content: Three-legged chickens, cats born with 1 eye, organs destroyed by tapeworms, these are just a few of the gross biological deviances that you'll see on display in this very strange and unsettling museum. Guided tours available.

voyage.name: Capilla de la Purísima Concepción
voyage.content: Built in 1521 under Cortés, this is believed to be the earliest Christian building in Mexico City.

voyage.name: Parroquia San Juan Bautista
voyage.alt: Church of St John the Baptist
voyage.content: One of the oldest churches in Mexico, it was built by Franciscan missionaries between 1522 and 1552. The church is spectacularly beautiful, built in a baroque style and elaborately decorated with interior architectural detail and historic artwork including paintings and sculpture. An interior courtyard and small side chapels offer space for quiet spiritual reflection.

voyage.name: Casa de la Malinche
voyage.content: Cortés had this house built for his Nahua mistress/interpreter, and many historians believe that he had his Spanish wife murdered here.
