Despite the house's historic and aesthetic significance, it is not marked by any plaques as many Mexicans today consider la Malinche a traitor. The building is not open to the public, but can be appreciated from outside.

voyage.name: Museo Frida Kahlo
voyage.price: M$320 (foreign adults), M$160 (Mexican nationals/residents), M$60 (students/teachers), M$30 (children/seniors); weekends: M$267.50 (adults), M$128.40 (Mexican nationals/residents), M$48.15 (students/teachers), M$21.50 (children/seniors), free (children under 6)
voyage.content: Also known as La Casa Azul, this walled hacienda painted brilliant indigo blue, is where the much-revered Mexican artist spent the last years of her life. Admission includes access to the courtyard, a small series of galleries with ever-changing displays, and the historical portion of the house, which has been preserved from the days when Kahlo was alive. A small snack bar and museum shop are also on the premises, an

voyage.name: Museo Diego Rivera-Anahuacalli
voyage.price: M$90 (adults), M$70 (Mexican nationals/residents), M$30 (students), M$15 (seniors/children 6-10); one ticket good at both here and Museo Frida Kahlo
voyage.content: Artist and muralist Diego Rivera built this structure to serve both as his studio and a museum to hold his collection of pre-Columbian art. The imposing neo-Aztec building sits in a parklike environment that is one of the few wildlife refuges in Mexico City. Guided tours of the main structure (in Spanish only) are given every hour or so. There is also a small gallery where art, music, and dance lessons, lectures, and

voyage.name: Museo Casa de León Trotsky
voyage.content: After being expelled from the Soviet Union, and subsequently from Turkey, France and Norway, Marxist theorist Leon Trotsky was granted asylum in Mexico, where he settled in Coyoacán in 1937. He continued to be vocally critical of Stalin's policies, however, and in 1940 he was assassinated in his home. The museum preserves the house in much the condition as it was in Trotsky's last days.

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Culturas Populares
voyage.price: M$13 (adults), free (concessions), free admission on Sundays
voyage.content: This museum offers homage to the many different indigenous cultures of Mexico, celebrating folk art, music, gastronomy, and more. They also have an impressive bookshop with art for sale from skilled artisans from all over the country.

voyage.name: Museo Nacional de Acuarela Alfredo Guati Rojo
voyage.alt: Alfredo Guati Rojo National Watercolor Museum
voyage.content: Housed in the former residence of Mexican artist Alfredo Guati Rojo, the museum is dedicated to preserving and exhibiting watercolor painting, by Mexican and international artists. Pieces in its permanent collection span from pre-Hispanic to modern times, and the building is a venue for temporary exhibits.

voyage.name: Museo del Automovil
voyage.content: Large museum with more than 4,000 square meters of exhibition space showcasing 120 historic cars dating back as far as 1904.

voyage.name: Museo Casa Kahlo
voyage.content: This is the home where four generations of the Kahlo family grew up and lived. Although Frida Kahlo was the most famous of Guillermo's children, he actually had an interesting life that ultimately had a big impact on Frida's worldview.

voyage.name: Cineteca Nacional
voyage.content: Designed by Mexican architect Manuel Rocha Díaz and completed in 1984, the Cineteca is dedicated to the preservation and showing of films in Mexico. This is a venue for current releases as well as classic films, and hosts a number of film festivals throughout the year.

voyage.name: Mercado de Coyoacán
voyage.content: A traditional Mexican market with a large selection of produce and food items as well as other goods; Frida Kahlo used to shop herself. There are also a number of food stalls here, making this a good place to stop for lunch.

voyage.name: Bazar Artesanal Mexicano
voyage.content: An arts and crafts market with good quality items.

voyage.name: Casa de Luna
voyage.content: Fair trade store that offers a beautiful selection of traditional Mexican folk art and an eclectic assortment of jewelry, textiles, Mexican-kitsch, nichos, Day of the Dead images, market bags, masks, milagros, etc. – varied but carefully curated. The upstairs gallery displays Mexican contemporary artwork.

voyage.name: Bazar Casa del Coleccionista
voyage.content: This place sells lots of vintage items, including china ware, toys, paintings, and ornaments.

voyage.name: Café Ruta de la Seda
voyage.content: Look for a small, green stucco building, without even a sign over the door, with the only indication that it's a cafe in this residential neighborhood are the tables and chairs out on the sidewalk. True to its hippie, progressive environment, this tiny cafe serves organic pastries and coffee, and has some Indian food on the menu (samosas, mango lassi). Try the green tea cake with ice cream, also made of green tea.

voyage.name: Café El Jarocho
voyage.content: This is a very old, family-owned coffee roaster's shop, and there are now at least three locations in Coyoacán. They have really good and cheap coffee, bad and cheap tortas (sandwiches in French bread), and reasonably standard American-style donuts. There are benches on the sidewalk just outside the Jarocho shops where you can sit to drink your coffee, or you can do like everyone else in Coyoacán and just stroll arou

voyage.name: Bizarro Café
voyage.content: A comfortable goth hangout. There is a really good bakery next door.

voyage.name: La Selva Café
voyage.content: A perennial student hangout, also serving baguettes and cakes.

voyage.name: El Morral
voyage.content: Very good Mexican food. Don't miss the chiles en nogada, large chiles stuffed with ground beef, raisins, and nuts, and covered with a nut cream sauce. Their hand-made tortillas are fantastic. Service can be a bit slow though.

voyage.name: El Jardin del Pulpo
voyage.content: The "Octopus's Garden" is a casual marisqueria, or seafood place, featuring ceviche, seafood paella, whole roast fish, and even fish and chips. Dining is cafeteria-style at long tables under an awning. If you want fresh juices, agua frescas, or ice cream, those are available from two shops next door.

voyage.name: Los Danzantes
voyage.content: Somewhat pricey modern international cuisine with twists on traditional Mexican dishes. They also bottle and sell their own brand of mezcál. Try the seafood-chipotle chili soup, the goat cheese-filled chicken breast with chipotle chili sauce, and, if you can afford the $200 price tag, the escamoles (ant eggs) sol azteca as a starter (small, but can be shared between two people).

voyage.name: La Coyoacana
voyage.content: Very good Mexican food and good drinking with the locals; Frida Kahlo and Diego Rivera used to spend time here. Don't miss the "Mole," "Michele's favorite" or carne tartara. Their hand-made tortillas are fantastic. Service is good, make friends with the Meseros; they are cool. Mariachis and a garden terrace also appeal.

voyage.name: La Bipolar
voyage.content: A tacky-fun restaurant/cantina owned by Mexican actor Diego Luna. Good place to go for drinks and a light meal. Try the shrimp burrito.

voyage.name: Taro
voyage.content: Probably the best Japanese food in Mexico City, owned by Japanese. Many Japanese people come here for lunch and dinner, so they attest to the authenticity of the meals – you won't find maki rolls with cream cheese here. Don't miss their spicy octopus entrée and the ice-cream tempura for dessert.

voyage.name: Taquería Aguayo 1
voyage.content: Just off of the Plaza Hidalgo, this little hole in the wall has some of the best traditional food in Mexico City. Their flautas are especially delicious, both the cheese (queso) and steak (barbacoa) variety. A tight squeeze (they don't seat very many), but well worth it, and very clean. An order of flautas (brings 4) is $28 MXN ($7 apiece – best deal anywhere for something this good); quesadillas and tostadas are $7

voyage.name: Las Nieves de Coyoacán
voyage.content: One of the best sorbets in the city. Try the ones made from exotic fruits: guanábana, zapote, maracuya, tuna (cactus fruit). The coconut-flavored paletas (popsicles) are also a treat.

voyage.name: Tepoznieves
voyage.content: Features excellent flavors such as Beso de Angel (angel kiss), Mil Floes (thousand flowers) and spicy sorbets!

voyage.name: Churrería General de la República
voyage.content: Churros are not too popular in Mexico City, but there are a number of places in Coyoacán (including street stands) that have them. The Churreria is a good place with excellent churros and you can fill it with a number of ingredients, like chocolate, fresa (strawberry), durazno (peach), lechera (milk), zarzamora (blackberry) and more.

voyage.name: Street food
voyage.content: The main plaza, at different times of the year, might have street food vendors that sell extremely good flautas (long, deep fried tacos), as well as buñuelos (deep fried sugar-coated bread), esquites, and elotes (corn with chile, mayonnaise, lime, and cheese).

voyage.name: El Chupacabras
voyage.content: These are some of the most famous street tacos in Mexico City. Their speciality is the chupacabra taco, a combination of pork, beef and a 'secret ingredient'.

voyage.name: El Hijo del Cuervo
voyage.content: Locals pack El Hijo del Cuervo which plays a mixture of rock and protest music.

voyage.name: Teatro Bar El Vicio
voyage.content: Cabaret venue that showcases music, theatre and cabaret shows. Shows are in Spanish.

voyage.name: Centenario 107
voyage.content: Fascinating and fun bar, grill, garden, and nightclub. Just 2 blocks from the Frida Kahlo house, it makes a great lunch spot. In the evening the place comes alive with a more party crowd. Good selection of craft beers and artesanal tequilas and mezcals. Outdoor garden area with tables.

voyage.name: Krystal Grand Suites Insurgentes 1991
voyage.content: Modern, upscale hotel on a busy thoroughfare. Not really in Coyoacan, but closest big hotel.

voyage.name: Hostal la Encantada
voyage.content: Barebones hostel for budget travelers. Excellent location, easy walk to mercado and zocalo.

voyage.name: Mansion de Papilio
voyage.content: Elegant small hotel set in a historic mansion. Gardens with roaming peacocks, large rooms with chandeliers etc. Service can be hit or miss.

voyage.name: Hostal Cuija Coyoacan
voyage.content: Budget hostel in a quiet residential neighborhood. Rates include free breakfast. 2-minute walk to Frida Kahlo House, 10-minute walk to Coyoacan Metro station.

voyage.name: Museo Casa Estudio Diego Rivera y Frida Kahlo
voyage.price: M$13 (general admission); M$30 (camera permit, no flash)
voyage.content: Diego Rivera's studio, where he also lived for some time with Frida Kahlo. It is a very interesting structure by famous Mexican architect Juan O'Gorman, consisting of two buildings connected by an aerial walkway.

voyage.name: Museo de Arte Carrillo Gil
voyage.content: One of Mexico City's finest modern art museums, based on the private collection of Carrillo Gil which includes well-known works by Diego Rivera, David Siqueiros, Rufino Tamayo, and Francisco Toledo. The museum also hosts temporary exhibits of contemporary Mexican and international artists.

voyage.name: Convento del Carmen
voyage.price: M$41 (adults), free (students/professors/children under 12); free admission on Sundays
voyage.content: An ancient convent where you can see the uncomfortable stone slabs where nuns slept, religious artwork, and, most importantly, a creepy underground crypt filled with mummified nuns. It is a truly enchanting old building, and connected to the Colegio de San Ángel.

voyage.name: Plaza del Carmen
voyage.content: The beating heart of San Angel with the historic convent adjacent to the plaza as well as San Angel's main marketplace. It is a gathering spot for locals and a pleasant park to sit and people watch.

voyage.name: Plaza San Jacinto
voyage.content: Site of the famous Bazaar Sabado, the park is just 2 blocks from Plaza del Carmen) is the hub of San Angel's arts community, with galleries and the Museo Risco adjacent.

voyage.name: Teatro de los Insurgentes
voyage.content: Built in 1953 by José María Dávila, this is one of the main venues for dramas and plays in Mexico City. On the façade of the building is a mosaic created by Diego Rivera, illustrating the history of theater and depicting the Mexican comedian Cantinflas as Robin Hood.

voyage.name: Teatro Helenico
voyage.content: Theatre in a historic Gothic chapel. Stages various plays and multi-disciplinary performing arts shows. Library on site. Small, intimate space.

voyage.name: Bazar Sabado
voyage.content: While always scenic, Bazar Sabado is the reason to head to the square, in front of a 16th-century church. It is one of the best crafts markets in town, where you can find original and high-quality art of all different regional styles, both traditional and more modern, and in all different price ranges. This is the best place to shop, people-watch, and just be happy.

voyage.name: Mercado de las Flores
voyage.content: A popular street market specializing in fresh flowers.

voyage.name: Mercado del Carmen
voyage.content: It's a traditional Mexican marketplace, but one adapted to the more Bohemian artsy lifestyle of San Angel. Whereas most marketplaces in the city open around 6am, the artsy crowd is just going to bed then, and they certainly won't be ready to go to a market until the sun is warm. The market opens at noon, but stays open later in the evening. The food hall is a star attraction, and while there are some traditional food

voyage.name: La Buena Fe
voyage.content: Comfortably upscale restaurant serving traditional Mexican cuisine. Good place for a business lunch or to meet a date for drinks.

voyage.name: Mallorquina
voyage.content: Comfortably rustic dining room serving classic Spanish cuisine (the paella is recommended). Flamenco show on Thursday and Saturday.

voyage.name: Carlotta
voyage.content: Nouveau Mexican cuisine in an outdoor terrace garden overlooking the Carmen church.

voyage.name: El Tizoncito
voyage.content: Street tacos with wood-fired trompo that makes for some of the best tacos al pastor in the city. Good place for late night munchies. The Sherezada Tizoncito is recommended.

voyage.name: Mama Rumba
voyage.content: One of the most popular dance clubs/bars in the city, usually very full, plays salsa, merengue, and other Cuban music. Can be hard to get into.

voyage.name: La Bipo San Ángel
voyage.content: Specializing in mezcal and live music.

voyage.name: Hotel Casa San Jacinto
voyage.content: An upscale colonial type of lodging with very rustic furniture and decor.

voyage.name: San Angel Inn
voyage.address: Desierto de los Leones 4058, San Angel
voyage.content: Business oriented long-term extended stay apartments.

voyage.name: Krystal Grand Suites Insurgentes
voyage.address: Av. de los Insurgentes Sur 1991, Álvaro Obregón
voyage.content: Clean, modern corporate style hotel with spacious rooms, on-site restaurant, Metrobus route in front of hotel.

voyage.name: Parroquia y Convento de San Agustín de las Cuevas
voyage.content: Church and former convent from the 17th century. Beautiful interior courtyard and grounds. Tlalpan used to be called "San Agustín de las Cuevas".

voyage.name: Parque Juana de Asbaje
voyage.content: Leafy park close to the zocalo. Shady walking paths and a modern children's playscape. Includes a nice Fondo de Cultura Económica book store and café.

voyage.name: Casa de Santa Anna
voyage.content: Previously, the home of Antonio Lopez de Santa Anna, Mexican president. Today, offices of an insurance company.

voyage.name: Tlalpan Mint
voyage.content: For 2 years, in the late 1800s, this building housed the Mexican Mint, today is a secondary school.

voyage.name: Cuicuilco Archaeological Zone
voyage.content: A large uneven circular pyramid (known as Pirámide de Tenantongo) is the most significant structure at these ruins, which archaeologists say is the oldest settlement in central Mexico, having been settled around 1400 BC. The pyramid itself dates from 800 BC, which is when the first layer of the pyramid was constructed (upper layers were not completed until as late as 600 BC). The pyramid also has a sub-basement, whic

voyage.name: Villa Olímpica
voyage.content: The housing complex used for the Mexico City 1968 olympics. There are a couple of other minor ruins from Cuicuilco inside the complex.

voyage.name: Ruta de la Amistad
voyage.content: The route of the Periférico was once used for large-scale sculptures by international artists made for the 1968 Olympics. After the construction of the elevated toll road over the Periférico, most sculptures have been relocated to the interchanges between Insurgentes and Viaducto Tlalpan with Periférico.

voyage.name: Heroico Colegio Militar
voyage.content: This is Mexico's foremost military academy, training army and air force officers. A separate academy in Veracruz trains naval officers.

voyage.name: Temple of the Asuncion Chimalcoyotl
voyage.content: Small community church dating back to the 17th century. Celebrates the feast day of the Virgin on December 8.

voyage.name: Church of San Pedro Martir de Verona
voyage.address: Enseñanza, Esq. Laurel S/n, San Pedro Mártir, Tlalpan
voyage.content: The original church was built by the Dominican missionaries in the 18th century. A new , very modern church was built next to it with a striking tent-like appearance. The older church is still used and has a number of noteworthy artworks, most striking of which is a painting depicting the death of St. Peter of Verona with an axe sticking out of his head. (Peter was murdered by a heretic in 1252.)

voyage.name: Parroquia de San Andres Totoltepec
voyage.content: This parish church was built between 1770 and 1773, it was refurbished in 1965. The church attracts pilgrims who come to celebrate the feast of St. Andrew in November each year.

voyage.name: San Miguel de Xicalco Church
voyage.address: 16 de Septiembre 1, San Miguel Xicalco, Tlalpan
voyage.content: This chapel, dedicated to St. Michael the Archangel, was built in the 17th century. The church contains a large stone sculpture of St. Michael. A small, unassuming but tranquil place to be.

voyage.name: Estadio Azteca
voyage.content: The largest stadium in Latin America is also the eighth biggest soccer stadium in the world. Built in 1961, it has an official capacity of 95,500 but frequently packing in several thousand more. It's the home of El Tri, the Mexico men's national team, and also home to two of the country's most famous soccer top-tier professional clubs: Club América and Cruz Azul. It also serves as venue for concerts and for occasiona

voyage.name: Six Flags Mexico City
voyage.price: 1-day tickets M$800, season passes start at M$1000
voyage.hours: varies by season and day, generally 10:00 - 18:00 (or later)
voyage.address: Carr. Picacho-Ajusco Km 1.5, Jardines del Ajusco
voyage.content: The largest amusement park in Mexico City. Roller coasters, thrill rides, shows and more.

voyage.name: KidZania
voyage.hours: Wed-Thu 09:00 - 15:00, Fri-Sun 11:00 - 19:00, closed Mon-Tue (but can vary for holidays)
voyage.content: A simulated city theme park where children can play and pretend to do adult jobs as they navigate through the child-sized city.

voyage.name: Mexico City Philharmonic Orchestra
voyage.content: This concert hall houses the Mexico City Philharmonic Orchestra, under the direction of Scott Yoo. There are concerts every weekend as well as other cultural activities. Weekend concerts are Saturday at 18:00 and Sunday at 12:30.

voyage.name: Parque Nacional Fuentes Brotantes
voyage.content: Forested area with natural springs just across Insurgentes Sur from the Centro Histórico.

voyage.name: Bosque de Tlalpan
voyage.content: A national forest (Natural Protected Area), it is a hilly forest 1 km west of the Centro Histórico. There are plenty of free courses and activities at the Casa de la Cultura (cultural centre). The impressive building facade was once located in the Condesa and was a pumping station used to bring water from Xochimilco to Mexico City.

voyage.name: Parque Ecológico Loreto y Peña Pobre
voyage.content: Green area in the springs of what used to be a paper factory. There is a restaurant, as well as examples of green technologies, such as rainfall capture systems and sustainable housing.

voyage.name: Parque Nacional Cumbres del Ajusco
voyage.content: Containing the highest peak in Mexico City (3,900 meters), the Ajusco National Park is a dense pine and oak forest that is home to small mammals, reptiles, and several dozen bird species. It covers an area of just under 1,000 hectares and natural mountain springs provide the source of the Lerma and the Balsas rivers. The park can be accessed by going South along the Picacho-Ajusco road from the Periférico. The road l

voyage.name: Volcan Xitle
voyage.content: Hiking trails go up to the top of the dormant volcano and also lead through cool forests to a natural cave, an historic ranching areas, and other natural attractions in the park. The Xitle volcano erupted in 245 AD, destroying the Mesoamerican city of Cuicuilco and burying the entire area of what is today the Pedregal district of Mexico City under a thick layer of lava flow. The eruptions continued for 70 years until

voyage.name: Parque Nacional Bosque de Tlalpan
voyage.content: Large forested area with walking paths. 5km jogging path. Picnic areas available. Sunday flea market. No dogs, bicycles or scooters allowed.

voyage.name: Mercado La Paz
voyage.content: This public market is one of the oldest in Mexico City and is the last "Porfirian" style that remains in Mexico City. Travelers interested in public architecture of the late 19th century will admire the elaborate brick facade, the black tile floors, and the stone pillars inside. As with all traditional marketplaces, it's a great place to buy fresh fruits and vegetables or authentic Mexican and regional prepared dishe

voyage.name: Perisur
voyage.content: The largest shopping mall in the South of Mexico City.

voyage.name: Plaza Cuicuilco
voyage.content: Shopping mall housed in a former paper factory.

voyage.name: ARTZ Pedregal
voyage.content: Large modern mall featuring art exhibitions, shopping, restaurants, a cinema, bowling alley, and indoor go-kart track.

voyage.name: Tetetlan
voyage.content: Luis Barragan, one of Mexico's most renown architects, designed this structure as a library that would integrate Pedregal's volcanic rock base with its natural environment to create a tranquil space for learning and study. The site was restored in 2017 and today operates as a casual traditional coffee shop and restaurant (lined with bookshelves that you can browse) as well as a holistic healing center offering yoga c

voyage.name: Michoacanissimo
voyage.address: Calle San Valentín 866, Pedregal de Santa Úrsula
voyage.content: Lively traditional Mexican restaurant specializing in birria. Locals recommend the birria de maciza. Nice variety of homemade salsas. Handmade tortillas. Live music.

voyage.name: Pancito Huipulco
voyage.address: Cda. San Juan Bosco 36, Huipulco, Tlalpan
voyage.content: Casual neighborhood restaurant serving traditional Mexican dishes including soups and guisadas, but the pancitas are the specialty.

voyage.name: Masa Azul
voyage.address: Av Renato Leduc 174, Toriello Guerra, Tlalpan
voyage.content: Small cozy restaurant with about 10 tables. Excellent breakfast packages for about M$200 including main dish, coffee, juice and rolls. If you're really looking to try some blue corn, order the masa Azul chilaquiles. Enchiladas are good here as are the breads and coffee drinks.

voyage.name: Antigua Hacienda de Tlalpan
voyage.address: Calz. de Tlalpan 4619, Tlalpan Centro I, Tlalpan
voyage.content: This place in the heart of Tlalpan in an estate from 1837 has a colonial feel with peacocks and big plates of food.

voyage.name: Sud 777
voyage.address: Blvrd de la Luz 777, Jardines del Pedregal
voyage.content: Elegant and sophisticated restaurant serving nouveau Mexican cuisine that is often a fusion of ancient ingredients with modern embellishments. Superb presentation and flawless service. A Michelin-starred restaurant.

voyage.name: Radisson Paraiso
voyage.content: 4-star hotel. Clean, spacious rooms with WiFi, cable TV, air conditioning. Next to Perferico.

voyage.name: Royal Pedregal
voyage.address: Periferico Sur 4363, Jardines en la Montaña
voyage.content: Upscale hotel with modern facilities. Spacious, clean rooms with a/c, WiFi, and cable TV. Indoor parking garage available.

voyage.name: Hacienda Pena Pobre
voyage.address: Camino a Santa Teresa 480-2, El Bosque, Tlalpan
voyage.content: Small boutique luxury hotel in a restored 17th century hacienda. Manicured gardens in the courtyard, high-end toiletries and linens. Cable TV, WiFi, air conditioning. Off-street parking available. 24-hour fitness center. Well-behaved pets welcome (additional fee).

voyage.name: Camino Real Pedregal
voyage.content: Modern, business-oriented tower hotel with clean, spacious rooms and attentive service. On-site restaurant available. Across a busy highway from the Artz shopping mall.

voyage.name: Plaza Uruguay
voyage.content: A small, nicely wooded park with a fascinating concrete sculpture in the middle; good place to stop and rest if you are tired of shopping.

voyage.name: Museo Soumaya
voyage.content: A private museum and collection owned by Carlos Slim, one of the wealthiest man in the world, according to Forbes magazine. The collection includes art from many well-known European artists, including an extensive selection of works by Auguste Rodin, and the building was designed by Slim's son-in-law, architect Fernando Romero.

voyage.name: Museo Júmex
voyage.content: This privately-owned modern art museum houses an extensive collection of work by Mexican and international artists, including Orozco and Amorales, and hosts special exhibits. Cafe and restaurant. The museum has ramps and elevators for access for people with limited mobility, and have wheelchairs available for loan free at reception.

voyage.name: Acuario Inbursa
voyage.address: Blvd. Miguel de Cervantes Saavedra 386, Amp Granada, Miguel Hidalgo
voyage.content: Large, very modern aquarium extending 5 floors below street level. 45 exhibition areas, including coral reefs, an Antarctic habitat for our tuxedo clad penguin friends, an enormous shark tank and many more.

voyage.name: Centro de Arquitectura y Diseño
voyage.address: Av Juan Vázquez de Mella number 481

voyage.name: Parroquia San Agustin
voyage.content: Grand modern and neo-classical church built of granite in the 1940s. The church was built by the Augustinians and features many architectural adornments. Spectacular shell-shaped entryway, vaulted nave, and a bright interior lit by many stained glass windows. The church has some excellent modern religious art including mosaics and a series of more than 20 paintings by contemporary Polish-Mexican artist, Anna Zarnecki

voyage.name: Teatro Angela Peralta
voyage.content: An amphitheatre on the east side of Parque Lincoln. Varied schedule includes concerts, plays, dance and other performing arts.

voyage.name: Hipodromo de las Americas
voyage.address: Av. Industria Militar, Colonia Lomas de Sotelo
voyage.content: Mexico City's home for horse racing, both thoroughbreds and quarter-horses. There are races nearly every day, the complex has different zones for different budgets including the original club-house and grandstand, with several restaurants and seating for 20,000 race fans.

voyage.name: Onora
voyage.content: High-end home design shop selling artesanal Mexican decor, ceramics, and tapestries. The shop has its own design service that can help you select harmonious pieces to create a theme for your living spaces.

voyage.name: TANE
voyage.content: High-quality silver, silver tableware, hollowware and other objets d'art, all handcrafted in Mexico.

voyage.name: Tienda MAP
voyage.content: Sells authentic Mexican folk art including eclectic trinkets that are not only visually appealing but an authentic piece of culture, often showing a humorous perspective on poverty, death, or other misfortune. The shop in Polanco is an extension of the official museum shop of the Museo de Arte Popular (MAP).

voyage.name: Piel Canela
voyage.content: Sells butter-soft leather handbags and accessories.

voyage.name: Antara Polanco
voyage.content: Mid to high-end shopping mall with food court and cinemas. Shops include Zara, Mango, Carolina Herrera and Hugo Boss.

voyage.name: Plaza Carso
voyage.content: Glitzy, modern mall with several restaurants A Ferrari dealership is here.

voyage.name: Plaza Polanco
voyage.content: Modest, dated mall

voyage.name: Pabellón Polanco
voyage.content: Middle class mall with modest stores such as Sears, has a food court, and cinemas. As of 2025, the mall is temporarily closed for renovations (more like a complete rebuild).

voyage.name: Liverpool Polanco
voyage.content: Huge classic department store where you can buy clothing, household items and an array of gourmet food and drinks.

voyage.name: El Palacio de Hierro–Polanco
voyage.content: Palacio de Hierro's Centro store is the historic flagship, but the Polanco store is very much the current flagship of the most upmarket Mexican department store chain. At 55,200 m² (594,168 sq ft), it is about half the size of Harrods or Macy's Herald Square, and as such, the largest department store in Latin America — perhaps the most luxurious as well. The chain promotes this branch as the El Palacio de los Palacio

voyage.name: Tianguis Sabado
voyage.content: Every Saturday, a pop-up flea market and art fair takes place in Lincoln Park.

voyage.name: El Pendulo
voyage.content: Eclectic bookstore with a widr-ranging selection of (mostly Spanish language) books with an integrated coffee shop serving hot and cold coffee beverages along with light food.

voyage.name: Libreria Gandhi
voyage.address: Av. Pdte. Masaryk 353, Polanco III Secc.
voyage.content: Mainstream bookstore with a good selection of Spanish language books, an excellent selection for kids, and a small section of English language books.

voyage.name: Un Lugar de La Mancha
voyage.content: Eclectic independent bookstore in a restored mansion with an outdoor garden and terrace where you can sit and have coffee with light breakfast and lunch food. Classy background music and friendly staff make it a hidden gem for CDMX book lovers.

voyage.name: Fisher's
voyage.content: Serves fish and shellfish in a casual and relaxed atmosphere. It is worth paying the slightly high prices due to the ample variety of shellfish that is found here and is not available at other places.

voyage.name: Rincón Argentino
voyage.content: Although somewhat commercial (the restaurant is outfitted like an Argentinian ranch), this restaurant is well known for its exquisite cuts of beef. It's a meat lovers paradise, although vegetarians are catered for with delicious salads.

voyage.name: Pujol
voyage.content: Contemporary Mexican cuisine in one of Mexico City's top restaurants, operated by celebrity chef Enrique Olvera. Reservations are a must and are usually made months in advance. Two stars in the Guide Michelin.

voyage.name: Suntory
voyage.address: Montes Urales 535, Colonia Lomas de Chapultepec
voyage.content: One of the oldest (and more traditional) Japanese restaurants in the city. The sushi is excellent as is the tepenyaki. There is another branch at Torres Adalid 14, Colonia del Valle.

voyage.name: Centro Asturiano
voyage.content: The Centro Asturiano is where some of the Mexican-Spaniards gather. It has an excellent restaurant offering delicious Iberian treats. A second location is in Coyoacan.

voyage.name: El Pendulo
voyage.content: Hip, bright, clean coffeehouse/bookstore with a wide selection of drinks, desserts, and light foods, plus shelves and shelves of (mostly Spanish-language) books and DVDs to peruse.

voyage.name: El Bajío
voyage.content: Some people call this the best place in the entire ciudad for traditional Mexican food. All of the tacos have a great flavor, and don't miss their mole sauce (even if on arroz). Bebidas buenoes - the horchata margarita and the cafe de olla are must haves. The restaurant is out of the way of the main Polanco area, but don't be fooled, it's usually busy so expect a wait.

voyage.name: Hacienda de los Morales
voyage.content: Historic and cultural space that operates as a traditional Mexican restaurant specializing in brunch, but with a spectacular dinner menu as well. Set in a large historic hacienda dating from the mid 16th century, the opulent estate features several spacious dining rooms, along with event halls and an outdoor garden. The hacienda originally operated as an agricultural estate growing olives and mulberries. As the city

voyage.name: Animal
voyage.address: C. Calderón de la Barca 108, Polanco III Secc
voyage.content: Contemporary restaurant with jungle motif. Innovative dishes and large, well-made cocktails. Start off with a selection of sushi or sashimi but save room because the steaks are huge. Big desserts are perfect for sharing.

voyage.name: Rosa Negra
voyage.content: Elegant restaurant with sophisticated menu featuring steaks and seafood. The colossal octopus and the wagyu beef steaks are favorites. The Taboo bar is a popular nightspot with DJs playing mostly electronic music, live musicians, and lively bartenders pouring creative drinks. Valet parking available.

voyage.name: La Cabrera
voyage.content: Argentinian beef restaurant that also serves pasta and other dishes. Casual but expensive.

voyage.name: Sylvestre
voyage.content: Elegant restaurant with valet parking, International menu.

voyage.name: Dawat
voyage.address: Av. Ejército Nacional Mexicano 676, Polanco III Secc
voyage.content: Modern casual restaurant serving Indian cuisine.

voyage.name: Quintonil
voyage.content: Elegant dining in one of the city's top restaurants. Locally sourced ingredients are used to stylishly present nouveau Mexican cuisine. Dishes include a chilayote in mole sauce and seasonal offerings. Reservations are a must. Two stars in the Guide Michelin.

voyage.name: Guzina Oaxaca
voyage.content: Celebrity chef Alejandro Ruiz grew up in Oaxaca and he celebrates his city's famed cuisine in this elegant traditional restaurant. Quesadillas stuffed with flor de calebaza are a great entrée, and the mole oaxaqueno is not to be missed. It is a deep black and redolent with chocolate and chile and its served over turkey (the traditional way rather than the modernized practice of using chicken). A Bib Gourmand selectio

voyage.name: Au Pied de Cochon
voyage.content: If you're an uber-billionaire landing your jet at Mexico City International at 3 in the morning, you are not going to one of the city's myriad late night taco shops no matter how bad the munchies hit you. Instead, you make a beeline to Au Pied de Cochon, a 5-star French restaurant in the heart of the city's ritziest neighborhood, where of course 5-star restaurants open all night, just like Denny's (if Denny's served

voyage.name: Bandido Cafe
voyage.content: Upscale nouveau Mexican cuisine served in a space where the quality of the music and sound system is as important as the aesthetics of the dining room and the presentation of the food. Specializes in grilled meats cooked over wood coals.

voyage.name: Ryoshi
voyage.address: Av. Pdte. Masaryk 111, Polanco Secc V
voyage.content: Elegant Japanese restaurant specializing in fresh seafood. Try the totoaba, tuna and hamachi. Sake samplers available.

voyage.name: Malix
voyage.content: Innovative regional Mexican cuisine featuring locally sourced heirloom foods that Mexico City foodies find in certain mercados and tianguis that were revealed to a wider world through the writings of the late British food journalist, Diana Kennedy. Celebrity chef Alonso Madrigal uses the distinctive flavors of indigenous ingredients to meld with traditional Mexican cuisine to create a unique dining experience.

voyage.name: Casa Portuguesa
voyage.address: Av. Emilio Castelar 111, Polanco III Secc
voyage.content: Trendy upscale restaurant serving Portuguese cuisine, like bolinho de bacalhau. Food is well cooked and portions are ample.

voyage.name: Cuerno Masaryk
voyage.content: Popular bistro restaurant serving contemporary Mexican and international cuisine. The bone marrow tacos are recommended as is the sashimi. Occasional live music.

voyage.name: Ivoire
voyage.address: Av. Emilio Castelar 95, Polanco IV Secc
voyage.content: Elegant French restaurant with casual outdoor sidewalk dining available. Excellent choice for a romantic dinner or for a memorable breakfast. In-house bakery.

voyage.name: Casa d'Amico
voyage.content: Comfortably elegant dining room where the kitchen serves authentic Italian pastas, pizza, steaks, risotto, desserts and more.

voyage.name: Auguri Kosher Trattoria
voyage.content: First class restaurant with elegant dining room serving kosher Mexican and Italian cuisine. Food is flavorful and service is friendly and efficient. Try the salmon carpaccio.

voyage.name: Vico's Grill Kosher
voyage.address: Av. Jaime Balmes 8, Polanco I Secc.
voyage.content: Classy restaurant serving seafood dishes, grilled beef, and Mediterranean cuisine.

voyage.name: Klein's
voyage.address: Av. Pdte. Masaryk 360B, Polanco III Secc
voyage.content: Hearty breakfast fare that includes fresh juices, classic Mexican dishes like chilaquiles alongside bagels and traditional Jewish dishes. Anything on the menu can be made kosher by request (extra charge may apply).

voyage.name: Blue bar
voyage.address: within Camino Real Hotel, Mariano Escobedo 700, Col. Anzures
voyage.content: A cool, relaxed place to have a drink and a nice chat. Average prices and good service.

voyage.name: Jaso Restaurant
voyage.content: Jaso is an ideal place for enjoying the finest Signature Cocktails in Mexico City surrounded by a cool ambiance.

voyage.name: Pinche Bar
voyage.address: Lago Iseo 296, Anáhuac I Secc, Miguel Hidalgo
voyage.content: Large warehouse bar attached to a Texas style barbecue restaurant. The bar has live music, comedians, drag queen shows and various other events.

voyage.name: Limantour Polanco
voyage.content: The Roma location established a reputation as one of the world's best bars (named to "50 best" list), so the newer Polanco location has a high standard to live up to. Fortunately, it's far easier to reserve a table at this location than the one in Roma. Creative mixed drinks with an emphasis on tequila and mezcal. Requires at least a nominal food purchase to order drinks.

voyage.name: La Santa
voyage.address: Av. Pdte. Masaryk 336, Polanco IV Secc
voyage.content: Exclusive upscale nightclub with pounding electronic music and multiple dance floors. Known for being hard to get into, especially if you don't look like you can afford to waste your money.

voyage.name: Cafe Toscano
voyage.content: Popular coffee shop with hot and cold coffee drinks as well as light food, including breakfast favorites like avocado toast and chilaquiles, a brunch menu (often accompanied by live music), as well as pizza and sandwiches.

voyage.name: Biscottino
voyage.content: Small coffee shop on one corner of Parque Lincoln with both indoor and outdoor seating. A variety of hot and cold coffee beverages are available as well as light breakfast and lunch plates. Locals love the fresh-baked cookies and vegetarians will appreciate the vegan muffins.

voyage.name: Cafe Joselo
voyage.content: Small coffee shop on the north side of Parque Lincoln with seating on 2 floors. A variety of hot and cold coffee beverages, but the Chai Latte is particularly recommended. A variety of baked goods are available and whole-bean or ground coffee is sold so you can brew the coffee at home.

voyage.name: Conejo Blanco
voyage.content: Casual coffee shop with outdoor tables on the sidewalk which are dog-friendly. In addition to the outstanding hot and cold coffee drinks they have their own French bakery with a variety of rolls, muffins, and savory breads. They serve a highly acclaimed French toast at breakfast.

voyage.name: Cafe Jekemir
voyage.content: Casual coffee shop with an emphasis on espresso. Serves good breakfast and lunch plates. More laid back than most Polanco places (with fewer fresas).

voyage.name: Hotel Camino Real Polanco
voyage.content: This 5-star hotel combines modern architectural profiles with obvious pre-Hispanic pyramid reminiscences. Architecture students visit the hotel to study the cutting edge work of architect Ricardo Legorretta, but everyone else visits because it's one of the city's top hotels with first-class service, posh restaurants and bars, and luxuriously appointed guest rooms. It has been the headquarters for two soccer World Cup

voyage.name: Habita Hotel
voyage.content: Boutique hotel with a minimalist interior, the Habita Hotel has changed the style of the Mexican hotel industry. White and grey/steel is a common colour theme, elegant gray Mexican marble lining the bathrooms from floor to ceiling. Located on the rooftop terrace, the hotel's AREA bar remains among the city's most popular nightspots.

voyage.name: Hotel Polanco
voyage.content: A local favorite that often gets overlooked amidst the grand hotels in Polanco, but still offers many of the amenities of larger hotels, but at a much better price. Pleasant furninshing and attentive staff round out a good deal. Across the street from República del Líbano garden (some rooms have garden views). Italian restaurant on premises.

voyage.name: Grand Polanco Residencial
voyage.content: Comfortable apartment hotel with large rooms in an older building. Off-street garage parking is available.

voyage.name: Dominion Polanco
voyage.content: Large, modern apartments with full kitchen. Busy neighborhood near bars, restaurants, shopping. Family friendly, pet friendly.

voyage.name: Alest Hotel
voyage.content: Tastefully elegant traditional boutique hotel with a large urban park directly across the street. Excellent on-site restaurant.

voyage.name: Las Alcobas
voyage.content: Posh luxury hotel. 37 rooms and suites with upscale furnishings. On-site 5-star restaurant and on-site spa.

voyage.name: Hotel Pug Seal
voyage.content: According to the editors of the Michelin Guide, the Pug Seal is Mexico City's top luxury hotel (it is the only hotel in the city with a Michelin Key designation). Housed in a 1940s era mansion in a residential area, the hotel features 20 rooms, each with unique features and furnishings. A full Mexican breakfast is served in the garden or on the terrace. Though expensive by Mexico City standards, the rates are a barga

voyage.name: Kimpton Virgilio
voyage.content: Elegant hotel with restored art deco architecture and traditional upscale furnishings. Rooms are small but comfortably furnished with boutique toiletries. Dozens of sidewalk cafes and 5-star gourmet restaurants within 100 meters. English-speaking staff.

voyage.name: Intercontinental Presidente
voyage.content: Large corporate hotel with spacious rooms, several restaurants and bars on site. Good breakfast including fresh fruit and sweet breads.

voyage.name: Casa Museo Leonora Carrington
voyage.content: Home and studio of surrealist feminist artist Leonora Carrington. Born in Britain, Carrington lived in this Mexico City home for 60 years -- almost all of her artistically prolific career. Carrington is difficult to classify. She worked in Mexico, but was educated and raised in Great Britain, so she had none of the sense of "Mexicanidad" (Mexican identity) that permeates most modern art in Mexico. She was a surrealis

voyage.name: Museo del Juguete Antiguo México
voyage.content: Huge collection of toys including dolls, action figures, model cars and trains, Barbies and lots more. Also provides walls to graffiti artists and is a popular place for urban artists to congregate.

voyage.name: Museo del Objeto (MODO)
voyage.content: Delightfully quirky museum of "stuff". All the things that become important to people in today's society, from toys, to car decorations. The museum is exhibition focused with changing themes a few times each year so the museum is "evergreen" and never the same place twice. It closes for several weeks every few months to change exhibits, so check their web site to verify that they're open and what the current exhibiti

voyage.name: Casa Guillermo Tovar de Teresa
voyage.content: Period home dating from 1910. Guillermo Tovar de Teresa was a respected intellectual in early 20th century Mexico and was a noted literary figure who chronicled life in Mexico City. The home and its furnishings, including an eclectic art collection, were purchased by the Carlos Slim Foundation. The home was restored and opened for public tours. It is operated by the Museo Soumaya (whose main museum is in Polanco). Al

voyage.name: OMR
voyage.address: Plaza Río de Janeiro 54, Col. Roma
voyage.content: Six to eight different exhibitions rotate throughout the year in this converted house in the heart of the Roma district, focusing on contemporary art by emerging Mexican artists.

voyage.name: 54 Gallery
voyage.content: Modern gallery showcasing contemporary art (often avant garde pieces in non-traditional media). Many of the works are by established international artists, but there are also some pieces by well-known contemporary Mexico City artists that are quite often better than the overhyped, overpriced pieces from New York or Europe.

voyage.name: MAIA Contemporary
voyage.content: Quiet 2-story gallery with a gorgeous spiral staircase. Features contemporary works by many of the city's most talented artists.

voyage.name: Mooni
voyage.address: Fernando Montes de Oca 43, Colonia Condesa
voyage.content: Casual gallery with friendly, informative staff. Affordable prices on a large selection of contemporary art, most by local Mexico City artists.

voyage.name: Parque México
voyage.content: The park at the center of La Condesa, the one that the neighborhood was built around, was once a horse racing track. The park was built in the early 1920s. The main square of the park hosts frequent music bands and they also have stalls selling handcrafts and clothing. The park has a famous fountain of a woman and also a clock erected by the Armenian community.

voyage.name: Parque España
voyage.content: This park was inaugurated on September 21st, 1921 to commemorate the 100th anniversary of the end of the Mexican War of Independence. It contains statues such as the monument to Lázaro Cárdenas. The park was designed by the pioneer of modern urban Mexico, architect José Luis Cuevas. It has a small lake with a rustic cement bridge that resembles a wooden bridge.

voyage.name: Fuente de Cibeles
voyage.address: Av. Oaxaca, Plaza de Madrid, Roma Nte
voyage.content: Roundabout on a wide avenue featuring a large fountain with a replica of a famous statue of a goddess in Madrid. The fountain is a gathering point for the Spaniard ex-pat community who come to celebrate Spanish soccer victories and similar events. The nearby tree-lined streets are full of restaurants and lively pubs.

voyage.name: Parque Rio de Janeiro
voyage.content: Attractive, well-maintained urban plaza ringed by historic buildings. The park features a replica statue of Michelangelo's David. The part is a pleasant place to walk or just sit on the park benches feeding the pigeons. Favored by local dog walkers.

voyage.name: Arena Mexico
voyage.content: Mexico City's most popular forum for Lucha Libre, the hugely popular wrestling sport of Mexico (and declared by UNESCO as part of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity). Matches are normally on Tuesday evenings and Sunday afternoons, but consult the website for current information.

voyage.name: Foro Shakespeare
voyage.hours: show times at 20:00 (see calendar for upcoming performances)
voyage.content: Despite the name, the theatre rarely performs in English and almost never anything by the Bard. Foro Shakespeare is a performing arts venue with three stages performing contemporary drama in Spanish by latino playwrights. The main stage (Primera) seats 190 patrons, Espacio Urgente seats 58, and the smallest space, Teatrino, seats just 38 in a very intimate setting. Foreign visitors will get the most out of it if they

voyage.name: ZiniK
voyage.content: You can find exclusive designs and best prices.

voyage.name: Librería Rosario Castellanos del Fondo de Cultura Económica (FCE)
voyage.content: One of the biggest bookstores in Latin America. Worth the stop just to see the gorgeous interior. You can spend hours just browsing through the shelves.

voyage.name: Cafebreria El Péndulo
voyage.content: Bookstore with a wide selection of books (almost all in Spanish, but a few English titles) and an on-site coffee shop. Many books on art and architecture.

voyage.name: Under the Volcano
voyage.content: English-speaking travelers might want to check out this bookstore which is the only one in Mexico City to specialize in English-language books. They also sell used books and will accept your already-read discards for partial store credit.

voyage.name: Casa Bosques
voyage.content: Stylish modernist bookstore with bright naturally lit interior and an eclectic selection of books and magazines in both Spanish and English. The best selection is books on architecture, art, and literature. If the door is locked, press the bell to get buzzed in. The store is on the second level.

voyage.name: El Hallazgo
voyage.content: Eclectic used bookstore with a wide variety of books on various subjects on many languages of the world. Very well organized with helpful staff who know how to find anything of interest. Also buys used books.

voyage.name: Mercado Alvaro Obregon
voyage.content: Along Alvaro Obregon Avenue, this market sells crafts, paintings and there is a unique stall selling fossils and meteorites.

voyage.name: Mercado Medellin
voyage.content: Fruit and vegetable market with a wide selection of unusual products used in Mexican regional recipes as well as cuisines from throughout Latin America. Many specialty vendors, some selling only chiles, others selling only coffees from Oaxaca, or food from Colombia. Street food fans will find regional dishes and inexpensive gourmet foods.

voyage.name: Mercado Roma
voyage.content: Large fun marketplace that specializes in food stands (grab-n-go, mix-n-match meals). Artesanal beers, gourmet coffees, a large variety of tacos...you name it.

voyage.name: Café La Glória
voyage.content: Reasonably priced Asian/Italian fusion with a Mexican touch, good bar and good coffee. The staff is laid back to the point of being unprofessional, don't worry about asking twice for your order. Try the pasta with chicken and sesame seed oil/soy sauce.

voyage.name: El Jamil
voyage.content: Lebanese meze restaurant serving grilled meats like kebabs and all your Middle Eastern favorites like hummus and tabouleh. Very popular.

voyage.name: El 10
voyage.content: Argentinian cuisine run by an Argentine owner, very good food at a very reasonable price. The bar is very popular at night.

voyage.name: El Ocho
voyage.content: This hip cafe has some good food and a pervasive retro look. Billing itself as a cafe recreativo, it's got sudoku and word searches on the placemats, and pencils and scratch paper on every table; help yourself to the wall of board games and magazines.

voyage.name: Esquina Común
voyage.address: Fernando Montes de Oca 86, Col. Condesa
voyage.content: Vibrant small rooftop restaurant in Condesa with innovative dishes that couple traditional Mexican dishes with unusual accompaniments and flavors. Editors of the Michelin Guide reserved their highest praise for the fresh fish entrees.

voyage.name: Frutos Prohibidos
voyage.content: This fast-food place serves rolled sandwiches using flat thin white bread. Wide choice of salads.

voyage.name: Green Grass
voyage.content: Fresh salads made to order with fresh greens and other ingredients. Ten locations in D.F. When you're missing fresh veggies, this is the place to go!

voyage.name: Hookah Lounge
voyage.content: The club serves Middle Eastern food and flavored tobacco "hookahs" at your table. The music selection is extremely good ranging from Electro-arabic, to house.

voyage.name: Parilladas Bariloche
voyage.content: This family-run restaurant is one of the cheapest places in the city to have good Argentinian/Uruguayan food. Start with some Provolone cheese and papas con amor (fried potato wedges with the peel still on). If you're hungry, also try the filete bariloche (for two people, about half a kilo of meat each), the bife bufalo or the arrachera.

voyage.name: Lardo
voyage.content: Creative Mediterranean food in a stylish restaurant owned by celebrity chef Elena Reygadas. Wood-burning oven. Lively corner location with open windows, plants and lots of light. Many unusual contemporary Mexican dishes like the insects mole. Variety of aguas frescas and kombucha.

voyage.name: Maque
voyage.content: Popular sidewalk coffee shop. Homemade pastries and outstanding people watching.

voyage.name: Baldio
voyage.content: Chic contemporary Mexican restaurant with an upscale clientele and a reputation for sustainable business practices that earned them a coveted green star in the 2025 Michelin Guide. The restaurant is not a "vegan" restaurant, but they heavily emphasize vegetarian dishes using locally sourced produce grown in the chinampas of Xochimilco. The restaurant claims to have achieved zero waste in their operations.

voyage.name: Gaba
voyage.content: Innovative upscale restaurant serving nouveau Mexican cuisine in an intimate setting. Service is top-notch and waiters will patiently guide diners through the sometimes unusual dishes. The tomahawk pork chops are big enough to share but too delicious to actually do so. Excellent wine list that includes suggested pairings for some excellent Mexican wines from Baja.

voyage.name: Vecchio Forno
voyage.content: A slice of Italy just a couple blocks from Chapultepec Park. Pizzas, homemade pastas, veal piccata, in-house bakery, gelatos and an excellent wine selection.

voyage.name: Los Loosers
voyage.content: A counter-culture vegan restaurant specializing in mushroom preparations and fermentation of all sorts, with inspiration from indigenous dishes.

voyage.name: Mendl Delicatessen
voyage.content: Classic Jewish deli with in-house bakery serving huge sandwiches. Assortment of bagels made fresh daily.

voyage.name: El Califa
voyage.content: Popular taco chain with various locations in Mexico City. A little overpriced, but very high quality tacos. The specialty is the gaonera (try the one with cheese), a large, thin slice of tender beef, roasted and placed on a tortilla. The house salsas are also notable for being made with fried tomatoes. After dinner, try the traditional Mexican coffee with cinnamon, café de olla.

voyage.name: BB Kfe
voyage.content: This small cafe offers excellent food at very low prices until 18:00. A set dinner includes a soup, a salad, a main dish, a small dessert, fruit flavored water, and coffee. The pasta dishes are good and portions are abundant.

voyage.name: Mog
voyage.content: Tasty authentic Japanese food at good prices in a very warm, randomly decorated place. A nice spot to hang out and have a drink or coffee/tea also. Impressive tea selection.

voyage.name: Las Flautas
voyage.content: Serves very good flautas and tacos de guisado. Delivery available.

voyage.name: Contramar
voyage.content: Hugely popular upscale seafood restaurant. Reservations recommended (can be made on opentable.com). Locals recommend the tuna tostadas.

voyage.name: Fishers
voyage.content: Lively fresh seafood restaurant with a wide range of innovative dishes. Excellent cocktails. Live music. Both indoor and outdoor dining areas (outdoor is sometimes more peaceful if you want to be away from the music).

voyage.name: Meroma
voyage.content: Trendy upscale restaurant serving nouveau Mexican cuisine. Modern, tranquil dining room. Good drinks, wide variety of dishes including beef, seafood, lamb and more.

voyage.name: Sartoria
voyage.content: Contemporary Italian cuisine in a sophisticated modern setting. Fresh house-made pastas. Sustainable locally-sourced ingredients.

voyage.name: El Pescadito Roma
voyage.content: Casual seafood lunch restaurant where you can get baja fish tacos at reasonable prices.

voyage.name: Rosetta
voyage.hours: Mon-Sat 13:00 - 23:00 (closes for 1 hour at 17:30), closed Sun
voyage.content: A definite "splurge" restaurant, Rosetta is an upscale gourmet dining experience set in an historic mansion with period furnishings, elegant dining rooms, and carefully hovering waiters. Innovative modern Mexican cuisine with equally innovative drinks and desserts. One of the city's top dining spots, so reservations are strongly suggested. Awarded a Michelin star.

voyage.name: Panadería Rosetta
voyage.content: A French-influenced bakery and cafe associated with the above restaurant, that quickly became famous for its flaky guava rolls. Get there early if you want a seat, as the line forms before it opens and doesn't let up, though it moves quickly for take-away pastries.

voyage.name: Maximo
voyage.address: Av. Álvaro Obregón 65 Bis, Roma Nte
voyage.content: Innovative contemporary Mexican cuisine with carefully considered dashes of French and Italian. Bright and inviting courtyard dining area. Awarded a Michelin star in 2025. Awarded Michelin's "Exceptional Cocktails" award in 2026 for innovative drinks like a corn husk martini. Reservations strongly suggested.

voyage.name: Salon Malafama
voyage.content: Trendy pool hall with a dozen billiards tables, cold beers, mezcal cocktails and a menu of burgers, fries, tacos and other light fare.

voyage.name: La Clandestina
voyage.content: Dark, intimate mezcal bar with an extensive range of artesanal mezcals and their own house brand, Enmascarado, which is available in bottles to go. A well-curated mezcal list explains a bit about the origins, manufacture, and sensory highlights of different mezcals. Excellent place to experiment with a sampler and learn a bit about the spirit.

voyage.name: GinGin
voyage.content: Popular cocktail lounge with upscale atmosphere and creative cocktails. Reservations are a necessity and the place has a reputation for "losing" reservations, and overcharging (so check the bill carefully).

voyage.name: Lagerbar Hercules
voyage.content: Taproom for a Queretaro-based craft brewery specializing in an eclectic collection of predominantly European style lager beers. The most unusual is probably the Rye Lager. They also have a nice Schwarzbier, seasonal brews like Oktoberfest, and a Mexican Lager intended to emulate a Corona or Tecate. Good selection of bar bites and the crowd is an eclectic mix of young professionals, ex-pats and digital nomads.

voyage.name: Mama Rumba
voyage.content: One of the most popular dance clubs/bars in the city, usually very full, plays salsa, merengue, and other Cuban music. There is another branch in San Angel, which is more popular with the younger crowd and can sometimes be hard to get into. Come early and get a free salsa lesson.

voyage.name: Licoreria Limantour
voyage.content: Claims to be "one of the world's top 50 bars", which seems rather dubious to me, but the cocktails are amazingly good! They have a wide assortment of spirits behind the bar with a mind-boggling selection of tequilas and mezcals. Upscale place with correspondingly upscale prices. Elegant atmosphere.

voyage.name: Tlecan
voyage.content: Small, intimate mescaleria that is just a few blocks from La Clandestina, with a similar focus and clientele, but a smaller, but exceptionally well focused mezcal list. Waiters are very knowledgable and can explain the types of maguey used by a particular brand and how it expresses itselfe in appearance, aroma, and flavor. In addition to outstanding artesanal mezcals from Oaxaca, they have a few bottles of mezcal sub

voyage.name: Jazzatlan Capital
voyage.content: Laid back club with a sort of retro-hipster vibe. The club is an offshoot of a popular club founded in Cholula. Features live jazz music nightly with an upstairs club (reservations required, can be made via Whatsapp) and a downstairs salon that becomes standing room only when a good band is in the house.

voyage.name: Janis
voyage.content: Popular rock-oriented club named in tribute to Janis Joplin. Lively crowd, large drinks. Be aware they add a 20% tip on all bills.

voyage.name: Mano Santa Mezcal
voyage.content: Hip contemporary bar specializing in mezcals with a wide variety of brands, many with very distinct flavor profiles. Many mezcal cocktails are offered including the classic mezcalhina, with a citric tang to it. Light bar snacks are available including a wonderful guacamole with chapulines (grasshoppers). A selection of local craft beers are available. English speaking staff available. Credit cards accepted.

voyage.name: Casa Franca
voyage.content: Fun, funky jazz club hidden away in an old house on a side street off Alvaro Obregon. Live jazz bands and great cocktails keep the crowds coming. Small club so reservations are a must, otherwise you'll be warehoused in an upstairs bar where you can't see the band. No parking available, but you'll be drinking anyway, so Uber itǃ

voyage.name: Falling Piano Brewing Co.
voyage.content: Large brewpub serving their house-brewed ales along with pizza, wings, and other light bar food.

voyage.name: Club San Luis
voyage.content: Lively club that attracts a lot of foreign visitors who come for the live salsa bands. Unfortunately, the management is erratic and has an unprofessional reputation.

voyage.name: Hippodrome Hotel
voyage.content: Boutique hotel in a historic art deco landmark, offering luxurious accommodations and first-class service.

voyage.name: Condesa DF
voyage.content: An amazing boutique hotel within walking distance of all the best bars, lounges, clubs and restaurants of Condesa. Also has a sushi bar rooftop bar, a chocolate lab, and a night club in the basement.

voyage.name: Hostel Condesa Chapultepec
voyage.address: Cozumel #53-A Col. Roma Norte (between Colima and Durango)
voyage.content: Hostel with shared dormitories. Cheapest lodging option in Condesa.

voyage.name: The Red Tree House
voyage.content: 16 beautiful units surrounding a peaceful courtyard. Rooms are reasonably priced and stylishly decorated. Many also have terraces. Breakfast includes the usual items plus a typical Mexican breakfast delicacy. Owners are friendly and very helpful with travel tips and assistance in arranging tours, etc.

voyage.name: Condesa Haus
voyage.content: Condesa Haus is a lovely building of 8 suites and rooms near the Patriotismo Metro station. Each accommodation is beautifully and stylishly decorated, and the staff are wonderful. Special discount (no tax or fees) if you pay cash.

voyage.name: La Palomilla
voyage.content: Comfortable and friendly bed and breakfast with eclectic decor and delicious breakfast included in room rates.

voyage.name: Brick Hotel
voyage.content: Upscale contemporary boutique hotel with first-class service and quiet, well-appointed rooms. Rooftop bar.

voyage.name: Hotel Lisboa
voyage.content: Large moderate hotel with spacious, clean rooms and good service.

voyage.name: Casa Decu
voyage.content: Architecture buffs will love the carefully restoration on this classic art deco landmark. The hotel is furnished with art deco style furnishings as well. Service is top notch and guests appreciated the rooftop terrace. Guests should be aware that the building does not have elevators or air conditioning, so if you need those amenities, another hotel might be a better choice.
